lessons.title: Unit 1 Overview — Complex Numbers
lessons.notes_html:
A complex number z = a + bi joins a real part a and an imaginary part b, where i = √(-1) and i^2 = -1. Complex numbers are added, subtracted, multiplied and divided part by part, and every one of them is a point (a, b) of the Argand plane.

The conjugate of z is z-bar = a - bi, and the modulus |z| is the distance of the point from the origin. In polar form the same number is written with its modulus r and its angle (argument) theta.

Formula: z = a + bi, with i^2 = -1; i^3 = -i, i^4 = 1

Formula: Conjugate: if z = a + bi then z-bar = a - bi

Formula: Modulus: |z| = √(a^2 + b^2), and z x z-bar = a^2 + b^2 = |z|^2

Formula: Inverse: 1/z = z-bar / |z|^2

Formula: Polar form: z = r (cos(theta) + i sin(theta)), where r = |z| and theta = tan^(-1)(b/a)

Key Points

  • Two complex numbers are equal only when their real parts are equal and their imaginary parts are equal.
  • Division is done by multiplying the top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.
  • √(-n) = i √(n) for n > 0 — always take i out first, then multiply.
  • For products and quotients in polar form: moduli multiply or divide, arguments add or subtract.
  • A quadratic with no real roots has two conjugate complex roots.

lessons.title: Exercise 1.1 (pp.10-11) - Real and Imaginary Parts, Arithmetic, Conjugate and Modulus
lessons.notes_html:
First read off the real and imaginary parts of a complex number, then practise the four operations. Addition and subtraction work part by part; multiplication uses i^2 = -1; division uses the conjugate of the denominator. The exercise ends with the conjugate and the absolute value (modulus) of a complex number.

In this exercise: 1. Separate the real and imaginary parts in the following. 2. Which of the following complex numbers are equal. 3. Simplify the following complex numbers. 4. Simplify the following. 5. Simplify the following. 6. Simplify the following. 7. Find the conjugate of the following. 8. Find the absolute value of the following.

Worked Example: 1. Separate the real and imaginary parts in the following: (i) 5 + 8i; (ii) 3/2 - (7/3)i; (iii) (2 + 3i)i; (iv) (7 - 8i)(1 + i); (v) √(2) - 18i; (vi) 3.

Formula used: z = a + bi; z-bar = a - bi; |z| = √(a^2 + b^2); multiply out and use i^2 = -1; for division multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

Step 1: (i) 5 + 8i is already in standard form: real part 5, imaginary part 8.

Step 2: (ii) 3/2 - (7/3)i: real part 3/2, imaginary part -7/3.

Step 3: (iii) (2 + 3i)i = 2i + 3i^2 = -3 + 2i: real part -3, imaginary part 2.

Step 4: (iv) (7 - 8i)(1 + i) = 7 + 7i - 8i - 8i^2 = 15 - i: real part 15, imaginary part -1.

Step 5: (v) √(2) - 18i: real part √(2), imaginary part -18.

Step 6: (vi) 3 = 3 + 0i: real part 3, imaginary part 0.

Answer: (i) Re = 5, Im = 8; (ii) Re = 3/2, Im = -7/3; (iii) Re = -3, Im = 2; (iv) Re = 15, Im = -1; (v) Re = √(2), Im = -18; (vi) Re = 3, Im = 0

Worked Example: 3. Simplify the following complex numbers: (i) (8 + 2i) + (4 - 6i); (ii) 3(2 + 9i) + (1 - 3i); (iii) (1/7 - (2/3)i) + (3/5 - (4/7)i); (iv) (12 + 7i) + (8i + 9); (v) (√(-3) + 2) + (13 + √(3) i); (vi) (8 + 15i) + (16 - 13i).

Formula used: z = a + bi; z-bar = a - bi; |z| = √(a^2 + b^2); multiply out and use i^2 = -1; for division multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

Step 1: (i) Add real parts and imaginary parts separately: (8 + 4) + (2 - 6)i = 12 - 4i.

Step 2: (ii) 3(2 + 9i) = 6 + 27i; add (1 - 3i): (6 + 1) + (27 - 3)i = 7 + 24i.

Step 3: (iii) Real parts: 1/7 + 3/5 = 26/35. Imaginary parts: -2/3 - 4/7 = -26/21. Result: 26/35 - (26/21)i.

Step 4: (iv) (12 + 9) + (7 + 8)i = 21 + 15i.

Step 5: (v) √(-3) = i √(3). So (2 + i √(3)) + (13 + √(3) i) = 15 + 2 √(3) i.

Step 6: (vi) (8 + 16) + (15 - 13)i = 24 + 2i.

Answer: (i) 12 - 4i; (ii) 7 + 24i; (iii) 26/35 - (26/21)i; (iv) 21 + 15i; (v) 15 + 2 √(3) i; (vi) 24 + 2i

Worked Example: 5. Simplify the following: (i) (2 - i)(3 + i); (ii) (3 + 2i)(3 - 2i); (iii) (2 √(-9) - 3)(3 √(-16) - 1); (iv) (3 - i)(4 + 3i)(5 - 2i); (v) (4 - 7i)^2; (vi) (i + 5)(7 - 6i).

Formula used: z = a + bi; z-bar = a - bi; |z| = √(a^2 + b^2); multiply out and use i^2 = -1; for division multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

Step 1: (i) (2 - i)(3 + i) = 6 + 2i - 3i - i^2 = 7 - i.

Step 2: (ii) (3 + 2i)(3 - 2i) = 9 - (2i)^2 = 9 + 4 = 13.

Step 3: (iii) 2 √(-9) = 6i and 3 √(-16) = 12i, so (6i - 3)(12i - 1) = 72i^2 - 6i - 36i + 3 = -69 - 42i.

Step 4: (iv) First (3 - i)(4 + 3i) = 12 + 9i - 4i - 3i^2 = 15 + 5i. Then (15 + 5i)(5 - 2i) = 75 - 30i + 25i - 10i^2 = 85 - 5i.

Step 5: (v) (4 - 7i)^2 = 16 - 56i + 49i^2 = -33 - 56i.

Step 6: (vi) (i + 5)(7 - 6i) = 7i - 6i^2 + 35 - 30i = 41 - 23i.

Answer: (i) 7 - i; (ii) 13; (iii) -69 - 42i; (iv) 85 - 5i; (v) -33 - 56i; (vi) 41 - 23i

Worked Example: 6. Simplify the following: (i) (3 - 5i)/(3 - 2i); (ii) (5 - √(-4))/(4 + 9i); (iii) (7 + 8i)/(9 - 2i); (iv) (√(9) - √(-16))/(2 + i); (v) (17 + 11i)/(6 + 5i); (vi) (6 + 7i)/(5 + 4i).

Formula used: z = a + bi; z-bar = a - bi; |z| = √(a^2 + b^2); multiply out and use i^2 = -1; for division multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

Step 1: (i) Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate (3 + 2i): (3 - 5i)(3 + 2i)/13 = (19 - 9i)/13.

Step 2: (ii) √(-4) = 2i. (5 - 2i)/(4 + 9i) = (5 - 2i)(4 - 9i)/97 = (2 - 53i)/97.

Step 3: (iii) (7 + 8i)/(9 - 2i) = (7 + 8i)(9 + 2i)/85 = (47 + 86i)/85.

Step 4: (iv) √(9) = 3, √(-16) = 4i. (3 - 4i)/(2 + i) = (3 - 4i)(2 - i)/5 = (2 - 11i)/5.

Step 5: (v) (17 + 11i)/(6 + 5i) = (17 + 11i)(6 - 5i)/61 = (157 - 19i)/61.

Step 6: (vi) (6 + 7i)/(5 + 4i) = (6 + 7i)(5 - 4i)/41 = (58 + 11i)/41.

Answer: (i) (19 - 9i)/13; (ii) (2 - 53i)/97; (iii) (47 + 86i)/85; (iv) (2 - 11i)/5; (v) (157 - 19i)/61; (vi) (58 + 11i)/41

Worked Example: 8. Find the absolute value of the following: (i) z = 5 + 13i; (ii) z = 13 - 18i; (iii) z = (5 - 12i) + (17 + 10i); (iv) z = (3 - 7i)(5 + 11i); (v) z = (7 + 8i)/(11 - 9i); (vi) z = (√(2) + √(-9)) - (√(8) - 4i).

Formula used: z = a + bi; z-bar = a - bi; |z| = √(a^2 + b^2); multiply out and use i^2 = -1; for division multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator.

Step 1: (i) |5 + 13i| = √(25 + 169) = √(194).

Step 2: (ii) |13 - 18i| = √(169 + 324) = √(493).

Step 3: (iii) z = 22 - 2i, so |z| = √(484 + 4) = √(488) = 2 √(122).

Step 4: (iv) z = 15 + 33i - 35i - 77i^2 = 92 - 2i, so |z| = √(8464 + 4) = √(8468) = 2 √(2117).

Step 5: (v) |z| = |7 + 8i|/|11 - 9i| = √(113)/√(202).

Step 6: (vi) z = (√(2) + 3i) - (2 √(2) - 4i) = -√(2) + 7i, so |z| = √(2 + 49) = √(51).

Answer: (i) √(194); (ii) √(493); (iii) 2 √(122); (iv) 2 √(2117); (v) √(113)/√(202); (vi) √(51)

lessons.title: Exercise 1.2 (p.32) - Equations, Factorisation and Polar Form
lessons.notes_html:
Here complex numbers are used to solve equations: simultaneous equations with complex coefficients, quadratics and polynomials factorised into linear factors. The second half changes numbers into polar form and uses it for products, equations and simple applications to waves and AC circuits.

In this exercise: 1. Solve the simultaneous linear equations with complex co-efficients: 2z + 3iw = 1 + i; (1 - i)z + w = 2 + i. 2. Solve: z + (z + i)w = 3i; 3iz - 2iw = 3 + 2i. 3. Solve: (3 - i)z + 2iw = 5i; z + iw = 7i. 4. Factorize the polynomials P(z) into linear factors. 5. Solve the quadratic equations. 6. Solve the equation in polar form. 7. Represent the complex numbers in polar form. 8. If z1 = 5 √(3) + 5i and z2 = 3 + 3 √(3) i then find z1 z2 in polar form. 9. Solve the equations for z. 10. Solve the following in-equalities (Polar form), where z is a complex number. 11. Two waves are represented by A = 3e^{i pi/6} and B = 2e^{-i pi/4}. Find the resulting wave amplitude after interference. 12. In an AC circuit, the voltage is represented by V = 20e^{i pi/3}. Find the real and imaginary parts of the voltage.

Worked Example: 1(i). Solve the simultaneous linear equations with complex co-efficients: 2z + 3iw = 1 + i; (1 - i)z + w = 2 + i.

Formula used: Polar form z = r (cos(theta) + i sin(theta)) with r = √(a^2 + b^2); equate real and imaginary parts to solve equations; a polynomial with root z0 has factor (z - z0).

Step 1: From the second equation, w = 2 + i - (1 - i)z.

Step 2: Substitute in the first equation: 2z + 3i(2 + i - (1 - i)z) = 1 + i.

Step 3: Expand: 2z + 6i + 3i^2 - 3i(1 - i)z = 1 + i, i.e. 2z + 6i - 3 - (3i + 3)z = 1 + i.

Step 4: Collect z: z(2 - 3 - 3i) + (-3 + 6i) = 1 + i, so z(-1 - 3i) = 4 - 5i.

Step 5: Therefore z = (4 - 5i)/(-1 - 3i) = (4 - 5i)(-1 + 3i)/10 = (11 + 17i)/10.

Step 6: Then w = 2 + i - (1 - i)(11/10 + 17i/10) = 2 + i - (28 + 6i)/10 = -4/5 + (2/5)i.

Step 7: Check: 2z + 3iw = 11/5 + 17i/5 - 12i/5 - 6/5 = 1 + i, as required.

Answer: z = 11/10 + (17/10)i, w = -4/5 + (2/5)i

Worked Example: 2. Factorize the polynomials P(z) into linear factors.

Formula used: Polar form z = r (cos(theta) + i sin(theta)) with r = √(a^2 + b^2); equate real and imaginary parts to solve equations; a polynomial with root z0 has factor (z - z0).

Step 1: (i) z^2 + 9 = z^2 - (3i)^2 = (z + 3i)(z - 3i).

Step 2: (ii) z^2 + 121 = z^2 - (11i)^2 = (z + 11i)(z - 11i).

Step 3: (iii) z^2 + 3 = z^2 - (i √(3))^2 = (z + i √(3))(z - i √(3)).

Step 4: (iv) z^2 + 196 = z^2 - (14i)^2 = (z + 14i)(z - 14i).

Step 5: (v) z^3 + 3z^2 + 4z + 2: z = -1 is a root (-1 + 3 - 4 + 2 = 0), so divide: (z + 1)(z^2 + 2z + 2). And z^2 + 2z + 2 = (z + 1 - i)(z + 1 + i).

Step 6: (vi) z^3 + 2z^2 - 2z - 12: z = 2 is a root (8 + 8 - 4 - 12 = 0), so divide: (z - 2)(z^2 + 4z + 6). And z^2 + 4z + 6 = (z + 2 - i √(2))(z + 2 + i √(2)).

Step 7: (vii) z^3 - 7z^2 + 19z - 13: z = 1 is a root (1 - 7 + 19 - 13 = 0), so divide: (z - 1)(z^2 - 6z + 13). And z^2 - 6z + 13 = (z - 3 - 2i)(z - 3 + 2i).

Step 8: (viii) RESOLVED from the book's Answers section (book p360): as printed, z^3 - z^2 + 17z + 15 has no rational root (P(-1) = -4, P(1) = 32, P(3) = 84, P(-3) = -72, P(5) = 200, P(-5) = -220), so it cannot be factorised as printed. The Answers section gives (z + 1)(z + 1 - i √(14))(z + 1 + i √(14)), which expands to z^3 + 3z^2 + 17z + 15. Hence the printed '-z^2' is a misprint for '+3z^2'. With the intended polynomial: z = -1 is a root, divide to get (z + 1)(z^2 + 2z + 15), and z^2 + 2z + 15 = (z + 1 - i √(14))(z + 1 + i √(14)).

Answer: (i) (z + 3i)(z - 3i); (ii) (z + 11i)(z - 11i); (iii) (z + i √(3))(z - i √(3)); (iv) (z + 14i)(z - 14i); (v) (z + 1)(z + 1 - i)(z + 1 + i); (vi) (z - 2)(z + 2 - i √(2))(z + 2 + i √(2)); (vii) (z - 1)(z - 3 - 2i)(z - 3 + 2i); (viii) (z + 1)(z + 1 - i √(14))(z + 1 + i √(14))

Worked Example: 5. Represent the complex numbers in polar form: (i) -1 - i; (ii) 1 + i √(3); (iii) 2 + i 2 √(3); (iv) √(6) + i √(2).

Formula used: Polar form z = r (cos(theta) + i sin(theta)) with r = √(a^2 + b^2); equate real and imaginary parts to solve equations; a polynomial with root z0 has factor (z - z0).

Step 1: (i) -1 - i: r = √(1 + 1) = √(2); third quadrant, theta = 5pi/4. Form: √(2)(cos(5pi/4) + i sin(5pi/4)).

Step 2: (ii) 1 + i √(3): r = √(1 + 3) = 2; first quadrant, theta = pi/3. Form: 2(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)).

Step 3: (iii) 2 + i 2 √(3): r = √(4 + 12) = 4; first quadrant, theta = pi/3. Form: 4(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)).

Step 4: (iv) √(6) + i √(2): r = √(6 + 2) = √(8) = 2 √(2); first quadrant, tan theta = √(2)/√(6) = 1/√(3), theta = pi/6. Form: 2 √(2)(cos(pi/6) + i sin(pi/6)).

Answer: (i) √(2)(cos(5pi/4) + i sin(5pi/4)); (ii) 2(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)); (iii) 4(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)); (iv) 2 √(2)(cos(pi/6) + i sin(pi/6))

Worked Example: 7. Solve the equations for z: (i) 10z - 8i = 1 - 5iz; (ii) (z - 3)/(z + i) = i; (iii) 4z - 3i = 1 + 3iz; (iv) (3i - 5z)/(4 - i) = z/2.

Formula used: Polar form z = r (cos(theta) + i sin(theta)) with r = √(a^2 + b^2); equate real and imaginary parts to solve equations; a polynomial with root z0 has factor (z - z0).

Step 1: (i) This is the same equation as Q4(i): z = 2/5 + (3/5)i (see Q4(i) for steps).

Step 2: (ii) (z - 3) = i(z + i) = iz - 1, so z - iz = 2, z(1 - i) = 2, z = 2/(1 - i) = 2(1 + i)/2 = 1 + i.

Step 3: (iii) 4z - 3iz = 1 + 3i, so z(4 - 3i) = 1 + 3i. Hence z = (1 + 3i)/(4 - 3i) = (1 + 3i)(4 + 3i)/25 = (-5 + 15i)/25 = -1/5 + (3/5)i.

Step 4: (iv) 2(3i - 5z) = z(4 - i), so 6i - 10z = 4z - iz, 6i = z(14 - i). Hence z = 6i/(14 - i) = 6i(14 + i)/197 = (-6 + 84i)/197.

Answer: (i) z = 2/5 + (3/5)i [same equation as Q4(i)]; (ii) z = 1 + i; (iii) z = -1/5 + (3/5)i; (iv) z = -6/197 + (84/197)i

Worked Example: 10. In an AC circuit, the voltage is represented by V = 20e^{i pi/3}. Find the real and imaginary parts of the voltage.

Formula used: Polar form z = r (cos(theta) + i sin(theta)) with r = √(a^2 + b^2); equate real and imaginary parts to solve equations; a polynomial with root z0 has factor (z - z0).

Step 1: V = 20(cos(pi/3) + i sin(pi/3)).

Step 2: cos(pi/3) = 1/2, so the real part is 20 x 1/2 = 10.

Step 3: sin(pi/3) = √(3)/2, so the imaginary part is 20 x √(3)/2 = 10 √(3).

Answer: Real part = 10, imaginary part = 10 √(3)

lessons.title: Review Exercise 1 (pp.33-34)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 1: conjugates, modulus, inverses and standard form, solving quadratics by completing the square, and polar form.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. Find the conjugate of (3 - 2i)(1 + 3i) / ((1 + i)(2 - i)). 3. Evaluate [i^20 + (1/i)^25]^3. 4. Reduce into standard form (1/(1 - 4i) - 2/(1 + i))((3 - 4i)/(5 + i)). 5. Solve by completing squares. 6. If z1 = 1 + 2i, z2 = 1 - i then find |(z1 + z2 + 1)/(z1 - z2 + 1)|. 7. If z1 = 1 + i, z2 = 2 - i then find. 8. Express each of the complex numbers in polar form.

Worked Example: 1(i). Conjugate of (1 + 2i)(1 - i) is:

a) 3 - i   b) 3 + i   c) -3 + i   d) -3 - i

Answer: a) 3 - i

Worked Example: 1(ii). |1 + i| / |1 + i| is equal to:

a) √(2)   b) 1/√(2)   c) 1   d) 2/√(2)

Answer: c) 1

Worked Example: 1(iii). Multiplicative inverse of a + ib is:

a) a/(a^2+b^2) + b/(a^2+b^2) i   b) a/(a^2+b^2) - b/(a^2+b^2) i   c) -a/(a^2+b^2) + b/(a^2+b^2) i   d) -a/(a^2+b^2) - b/(a^2+b^2) i

Answer: b) a/(a^2+b^2) - b/(a^2+b^2) i

Worked Example: 1(iv). Factors of z^2 + 256 are:

a) (z + 16i)(z + 16i)   b) (z - 16i)(z - 16i)   c) (z + 16i)(z - 16i)   d) (z - 16i)(z - 16)

Answer: c) (z + 16i)(z - 16i)

Worked Example: 1(v). Conjugate of (1 + i)/(1 - i) is:

a) 1   b) i   c) -i   d) 1 + i

Answer: c) -i

Worked Example: 1(vi). Absolute value of (2 + i)(2 - i) + 1 is:

a) 6   b) -36   c) 36   d) 36 + i

Answer: a) 6

Worked Example: 1(vii). (3 + i)/(2 + i) is equal to:

a) 7/5 - (1/5)i   b) 7 - i   c) 3 + i   d) (7 + i)/5

Answer: a) 7/5 - (1/5)i

Worked Example: 1(viii). If z1 = 4 - 3i, and z2 = 5 + 7i then Im(z1 + z2) is:

a) 4   b) 4i   c) -4   d) -4i

Answer: a) 4

Worked Example: 1(ix). Factors of z^2 + 169 are:

a) (z + 13)(z - 13)   b) (z + 14)(z - 14i)   c) (z - 13)(z + 13i)   d) (z - 13i)(z + 13i)

Answer: d) (z - 13i)(z + 13i)

Worked Example: 1(x). Standard form of (2 + 3i)/(2 - i) is:

a) 1/5 + (8/5)i   b) 1/5 - 8i   c) 15 - (8/5)i   d) 5 + 8i

Answer: a) 1/5 + (8/5)i

Worked Example: 2. Find the conjugate of (3 - 2i)(1 + 3i) / ((1 + i)(2 - i)).

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 1 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: Numerator: (3 - 2i)(1 + 3i) = 3 + 9i - 2i - 6i^2 = 9 + 7i.

Step 2: Denominator: (1 + i)(2 - i) = 2 - i + 2i - i^2 = 3 + i.

Step 3: Quotient: (9 + 7i)/(3 + i) = (9 + 7i)(3 - i)/10 = (34 + 12i)/10 = 17/5 + (6/5)i.

Step 4: The conjugate changes the sign of the imaginary part: 17/5 - (6/5)i.

Answer: 17/5 - (6/5)i

Worked Example: 4. Reduce into standard form (1/(1 - 4i) - 2/(1 + i))((3 - 4i)/(5 + i)).

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 1 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: 1/(1 - 4i) = (1 + 4i)/17. 2/(1 + i) = 2(1 - i)/2 = 1 - i.

Step 2: Difference: (1 + 4i)/17 - (1 - i) = (1 + 4i - 17 + 17i)/17 = (-16 + 21i)/17.

Step 3: (3 - 4i)/(5 + i) = (3 - 4i)(5 - i)/26 = (11 - 23i)/26.

Step 4: Product: (-16 + 21i)(11 - 23i)/(17 x 26) = (307 + 599i)/442 = 307/442 + (599/442)i.

Answer: 307/442 + (599/442)i

Worked Example: 5. Solve by completing squares: (i) 3z^2 - 15z = 21; (ii) 2z^2 = -3z - 15.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 1 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: (i) Divide by 3: z^2 - 5z = 7. Complete the square: (z - 5/2)^2 = 7 + 25/4 = 53/4. So z = 5/2 +- √(53)/2.

Step 2: (ii) Divide by 2: z^2 + (3/2)z = -15/2. Complete the square: (z + 3/4)^2 = -15/2 + 9/16 = -111/16. So z = -3/4 +- i √(111)/4.

Answer: (i) z = 5/2 +- √(53)/2; (ii) z = -3/4 +- i √(111)/4

Worked Example: 6. If z1 = 1 + 2i, z2 = 1 - i then find |(z1 + z2 + 1)/(z1 - z2 + 1)|.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 1 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: z1 + z2 + 1 = (1 + 2i) + (1 - i) + 1 = 3 + i.

Step 2: z1 - z2 + 1 = (1 + 2i) - (1 - i) + 1 = 1 + 3i.

Step 3: The quotient has modulus |3 + i|/|1 + 3i| = √(10)/√(10) = 1.

Answer: 1

Worked Example: 8. Express each of the complex numbers in polar form: (i) -√(5) - √(5) i; (ii) -1/2 - (√(3)/2) i.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 1 Overview and Lessons 1 to 2 of this unit.

Step 1: (i) -√(5) - √(5) i: r = √(5 + 5) = √(10); third quadrant, theta = 5pi/4. Form: √(10)(cos(5pi/4) + i sin(5pi/4)).

Step 2: (ii) -1/2 - (√(3)/2) i: r = √(1/4 + 3/4) = 1; third quadrant, theta = 4pi/3. Form: cos(4pi/3) + i sin(4pi/3).

Answer: (i) √(10)(cos(5pi/4) + i sin(5pi/4)); (ii) cos(4pi/3) + i sin(4pi/3)

lessons.title: Unit 2 Overview — Matrices and Determinants
lessons.notes_html:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers; its order is rows x columns. Matrices of the same order add and subtract entry by entry, and the product AB is defined when the columns of A match the rows of B — each entry of AB is a row of A dotted with a column of B.

The determinant |A| of a square matrix is a single number. It gives the inverse A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A| (when |A| is not zero) and drives the methods of this unit for solving linear systems: echelon forms, matrix inversion, Cramer’s rule, Gaussian elimination and Gauss-Jordan.

Formula: (AB)^t = B^t A^t and (A + B)^t = A^t + B^t

Formula: Inverse: A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|, defined only when |A| is not 0

Formula: Cramer’s rule: x = Dx / D, y = Dy / D, z = Dz / D

Formula: Rank: the number of non-zero rows in echelon form

Formula: A system AX = B has a unique solution exactly when |A| is not 0

Key Points

  • Matrix multiplication is not commutative: AB is usually not BA.
  • The cofactor of an entry is (-1)^(i+j) times its minor — the checkerboard of signs starts with + at the (1,1) entry.
  • Swapping two rows changes the sign of a determinant; a row of zeros, or two equal rows, makes it zero.
  • A homogeneous system always has the trivial solution; it has more solutions exactly when the determinant is zero.
  • In reduced echelon form every pivot is 1 and the only non-zero entry of its column.

lessons.title: Exercise 2.1 (p.46) - Matrix Arithmetic and the Transpose
lessons.notes_html:
Addition, subtraction, scalar multiples and products of matrices, with the identity matrix I. The last questions prove the transpose rules: (A^t)^t = A and (AB)^t = B^t A^t.

In this exercise: 1. If A = [[1, 3, 7], [1, 4, 5], [2, 3, 6]] and B = [[3, -1, 1], [1, 1, 3], [2, 4, 5]], then find. 2. If A = [[1, 4], [3, 5]], B = [[-3, 2], [1, 4]] and C = [[1, 0], [3, 2]], then find A^2 + BC. 3. If A = [[4, -2], [-3, 6]], B = [[0, 2], [1, 3]] and C = [[-2, 3], [1, 4]], then find. 4. If A = [[4, 2i, 3], [i, 4, 1], [3, -5, 6]] and B = [[3i, 2, 1], [-2, 7i, 3], [2i, 3, 8]], then find. 5. If A = [[5, 3, 1], [-2, 1, 4], [1, 3, -2]], then show that A I_3 = A. 6. If A = [[3, 1, 2], [2, 1, 6], [4, 2, 1]], B = [[3, -1, 2], [2, 1, 4], [1, 5, 4]], then show that. 7. If C = [[5, -3], [2, 7]], D = [[2, -3/2], [1, 3]] then show that; C - 2D = I_2. 8. If A = [[3, 1, 2], [2, 1, 5], [4, 1, 6]], B = [[1, 0, -2], [3, 1, 0], [0, 2, 1]] then show that. 9. If A = [[sin^2(theta), -cos(theta)], [sin(theta), cos^2(theta)]], B = [[cos^2(theta), cos(theta)], [sin(theta), sin^2(theta)]] then show that; A + B = I_2.

Worked Example: 1. If A = [[1, 3, 7], [1, 4, 5], [2, 3, 6]] and B = [[3, -1, 1], [1, 1, 3], [2, 4, 5]], then find (i) 3A - 4B (ii) A + 3(B - A).

Formula used: Add or subtract entry by entry; for AB, entry (i, j) = (row i of A) . (column j of B); the transpose turns rows into columns.

Step 1: (i) 3A = [[3, 9, 21], [3, 12, 15], [6, 9, 18]] and 4B = [[12, -4, 4], [4, 4, 12], [8, 16, 20]]. Subtracting: 3A - 4B = [[-9, 13, 17], [-1, 8, 3], [-2, -7, -2]].

Step 2: (ii) B - A = [[2, -4, -6], [0, -3, -2], [0, 1, -1]], so 3(B - A) = [[6, -12, -18], [0, -9, -6], [0, 3, -3]]. Adding A: A + 3(B - A) = [[7, -9, -11], [1, -5, -1], [2, 6, 3]].

Answer: (i) [[-9, 13, 17], [-1, 8, 3], [-2, -7, -2]]; (ii) [[7, -9, -11], [1, -5, -1], [2, 6, 3]]

Worked Example: 3. If A = [[4, -2], [-3, 6]], B = [[0, 2], [1, 3]] and C = [[-2, 3], [1, 4]], then find (i) A^2 (ii) BC (iii) B^2 - AB.

Formula used: Add or subtract entry by entry; for AB, entry (i, j) = (row i of A) . (column j of B); the transpose turns rows into columns.

Step 1: (i) A^2 = [[16 + 6, -8 - 12], [-12 - 18, 6 + 36]] = [[22, -20], [-30, 42]].

Step 2: (ii) BC = [[0 + 2, 0 + 8], [-2 + 3, 3 + 12]] = [[2, 8], [1, 15]].

Step 3: (iii) B^2 = [[2, 6], [3, 11]] and AB = [[-2, 2], [6, 12]], so B^2 - AB = [[4, 4], [-3, -1]].

Answer: (i) [[22, -20], [-30, 42]]; (ii) [[2, 8], [1, 15]]; (iii) [[4, 4], [-3, -1]]

Worked Example: 5. If A = [[5, 3, 1], [-2, 1, 4], [1, 3, -2]], then show that A I_3 = A.

Formula used: Add or subtract entry by entry; for AB, entry (i, j) = (row i of A) . (column j of B); the transpose turns rows into columns.

Step 1: Multiplying by the identity leaves every row unchanged: A I_3 = [[5, 3, 1], [-2, 1, 4], [1, 3, -2]] = A.

Answer: A I_3 = A is shown

Worked Example: 7. If C = [[5, -3], [2, 7]], D = [[2, -3/2], [1, 3]] then show that; C - 2D = I_2.

Formula used: Add or subtract entry by entry; for AB, entry (i, j) = (row i of A) . (column j of B); the transpose turns rows into columns.

Step 1: 2D = [[4, -3], [2, 6]]. Hence C - 2D = [[5 - 4, -3 + 3], [2 - 2, 7 - 6]] = [[1, 0], [0, 1]] = I_2.

Answer: C - 2D = I_2 is shown

Worked Example: 9. If A = [[sin^2(theta), -cos(theta)], [sin(theta), cos^2(theta)]], B = [[cos^2(theta), cos(theta)], [sin(theta), sin^2(theta)]] then show that; A + B = I_2. (Flag: as printed this is FALSE. A + B = [[1, 0], [2sin(theta), 1]], which equals I_2 only when sin(theta) = 0. The (2,1) entries add to 2sin(theta), not 0.)

Formula used: Add or subtract entry by entry; for AB, entry (i, j) = (row i of A) . (column j of B); the transpose turns rows into columns.

Step 1: Adding entry by entry: (1,1): sin^2(theta) + cos^2(theta) = 1. (1,2): -cos(theta) + cos(theta) = 0. (2,1): sin(theta) + sin(theta) = 2sin(theta). (2,2): cos^2(theta) + sin^2(theta) = 1.

Step 2: Hence A + B = [[1, 0], [2sin(theta), 1]]. This is I_2 only if sin(theta) = 0; the book's claim as printed is incorrect.

Answer: A + B = [[1, 0], [2sin(theta), 1]] — NOT I_2 in general (see flag)

lessons.title: Exercise 2.2 (p.59) - Determinants by Cofactors and Their Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Evaluate 3x3 determinants by cofactor expansion, then prove determinant identities without expanding — use row and column operations: equal or proportional rows give zero, and a column that is a sum can be split.

In this exercise: 1. Evaluate determinant of the following matrices using cofactors. 2. Using the properties of determinants, prove the following without expanding. 3. Using the properties of determinants, prove the following determinants.

Worked Example: 1. Evaluate determinant of the following matrices using cofactors. (i) [[7, 5, -9], [3, 6, -1], [2, 4, -6]]; (ii) [[5, 2, 1], [-3, 1, 2], [-1, 2, 5]]; (iii) [[4, 2, 2], [7, 3, 4], [1, -2, 7]]; (iv) [[2, -1, 7], [3, 1, 8], [4, -5, 13]]; (v) [[1, 3, -5], [4, 7, 2], [-6, 0, 1]].

Formula used: Expand along any row or column with signs + - + / - + - / + - +; properties: two equal rows give 0; adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the value.

Step 1: (i) Expanding by row 1: 7(6 x -6 - (-1) x 4) - 5(3 x -6 - (-1) x 2) + (-9)(3 x 4 - 6 x 2) = 7(-32) - 5(-16) - 9(0) = -224 + 80 = -144.

Step 2: (ii) Expanding by row 1: 5(1 x 5 - 2 x 2) - 2(-3 x 5 - 2 x -1) + 1(-3 x 2 - 1 x -1) = 5(1) - 2(-13) + 1(-5) = 5 + 26 - 5 = 26.

Step 3: (iii) Expanding by row 1: 4(3 x 7 - 4 x -2) - 2(7 x 7 - 4 x 1) + 2(7 x -2 - 3 x 1) = 4(29) - 2(45) + 2(-17) = 116 - 90 - 34 = -8.

Step 4: (iv) Expanding by row 1: 2(1 x 13 - 8 x -5) + 1(3 x 13 - 8 x 4) + 7(3 x -5 - 1 x 4) = 2(53) + 1(7) + 7(-19) = 106 + 7 - 133 = -20.

Step 5: (v) Expanding by row 1: 1(7 x 1 - 2 x 0) - 3(4 x 1 - 2 x -6) + (-5)(4 x 0 - 7 x -6) = 7 - 3(16) - 5(42) = 7 - 48 - 210 = -251.

Answer: (i) -144; (ii) 26; (iii) -8; (iv) -20; (v) -251

Worked Example: 2. Using the properties of determinants, prove the following without expanding. (i) |x, a, x+a; y, b, y+b; z, c, z+c| = 0; (ii) |0, a, -b; -a, 0, -c; b, c, 0| = 0; (iii) |2, 7, 65; 3, 8, 75; 5, 9, 86| = 0; (iv) |a-b, b-c, c-a; b-c, c-a, a-b; c-a, a-b, b-c| = 0; (v) |sin^2(alpha), cos^2(alpha), cos^2(alpha); sin^2(beta), cos^2(beta), cos^2(beta); sin^2(gamma), cos^2(gamma), cos^2(gamma)| = 0; (vi) |(a+b)^2, a^2+b^2, ab; (c+d)^2, c^2+d^2, cd; (g+h)^2, g^2+h^2, gh| = 0; (vii) |a, a^2, a/(bc); b, b^2, b/(ca); c, c^2, c/(ab)| = 0.

Formula used: Expand along any row or column with signs + - + / - + - / + - +; properties: two equal rows give 0; adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the value.

Step 1: (i) Column 3 = column 1 + column 2, so the determinant is 0.

Step 2: (ii) The matrix is skew-symmetric (A^t = -A), so its determinant is 0.

Step 3: (iii) Column 3 = column 1 + 9 x column 2 (check: 2 + 63 = 65, 3 + 72 = 75, 5 + 81 = 86), so the determinant is 0.

Step 4: (iv) Column 1 + column 2 + column 3 = 0 in every row, so the determinant is 0.

Step 5: (v) Column 2 and column 3 are identical, so the determinant is 0.

Step 6: (vi) Column 1 = column 2 + 2 x column 3, since (a+b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab, and similarly for the other rows, so the determinant is 0.

Step 7: (vii) Column 3 = column 2 divided by abc, since a/(bc) = a^2/(abc), and similarly for the other rows, so the determinant is 0.

Answer: All seven determinants are 0, by the column relations shown

Worked Example: 3. Using the properties of determinants, prove the following determinants. (i) |-a^2, ab, ac; ba, -b^2, bc; ca, cb, -c^2| = 4a^2 b^2 c^2; (ii) |1, 1, 1; a, b, c; a^3, b^3, c^3| = (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a+b+c); (iii) |x, x^2, yz; y, y^2, zx; z, z^2, xy| = (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)(xy+yz+zx); (iv) |x+4, 2x, 2x; 2x, x+4, 2x; 2x, 2x, x+4| = (5x+4)(4-x)^2; (v) |a-b-c, 2a, 2a; 2b, b-c-a, 2b; 2c, 2c, c-a-b| = (a+b+c)^3.

Formula used: Expand along any row or column with signs + - + / - + - / + - +; properties: two equal rows give 0; adding a multiple of one row to another does not change the value.

Step 1: (i) Take a, b, c common from rows 1, 2, 3: determinant = abc x |-a, b, c; a, -b, c; a, b, -c|. Expanding the second determinant: -a(bc - bc) - b(-ac - ac) + c(ab + ab) = 4abc. Total: 4a^2 b^2 c^2.

Step 2: (ii) Apply C2 - C1 and C3 - C1, take (b - a) and (c - a) common, then the remaining 2x2 determinant is (c - a)(a + b + c) - (b - a)(a + b + c) up to sign; simplifying gives (a - b)(b - c)(c - a)(a + b + c).

Step 3: (iii) The determinant is 0 when x = y, y = z or z = x (two rows equal), so (x - y)(y - z)(z - x) divides it. It is of degree 4, so the remaining factor is a symmetric polynomial of degree 1, namely xy + yz + zx; comparing the coefficient of x^2 y z gives 1.

Step 4: (iv) Adding columns 2 and 3 to column 1 gives 5x + 4 in every row of column 1; take it out, then R2 - R1 and R3 - R1 leave a triangular determinant (4 - x)^2. Total: (5x + 4)(4 - x)^2.

Step 5: (v) Adding rows 2 and 3 to row 1 gives a + b + c in every column of row 1; take it out, then C2 - C1 and C3 - C1 leave a triangular determinant (a + b + c)^2. Total: (a + b + c)^3.

Answer: (i) 4a^2 b^2 c^2; (ii) (a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a+b+c); (iii) (x-y)(y-z)(z-x)(xy+yz+zx); (iv) (5x+4)(4-x)^2; (v) (a+b+c)^3

lessons.title: Exercise 2.3 (p.68) - Echelon Forms, Rank and the Inverse
lessons.notes_html:
Row operations reduce a matrix to echelon form and then to reduced echelon form. Counting the non-zero rows gives the rank, and carrying the same operations on [A | I] gives the inverse — also found here by the adjoint method for comparison.

In this exercise: 1. Reduce the following matrices into echelon form. 2. Reduce the following matrices into reduced echelon form. 3. Find rank by using row operations. 4. Find the inverse by using row operations and by adjoint method.

Worked Example: 1. Reduce the following matrices into echelon form. (i) [[1, 2, -1], [2, 4, 1], [3, 6, 2]]; (ii) [[2, 3, -1], [4, 5, 3], [6, 2, 1]]; (iii) [[1, -3, 2], [4, 5, 3], [2, 1, 5]]; (iv) [[1, -1, 3], [0, 3, 2], [2, -4, 1]]. (Note: echelon form is not unique — row scalings of these forms are equally valid.)

Formula used: Row operations: swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero number, add a multiple of one row to another; A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|.

Step 1: (i) R2 - 2R1 = [0, 0, 3]; R3 - 3R1 = [0, 0, 5]; R3 - (5/3)R2 = [0, 0, 0]. Echelon form: [[1, 2, -1], [0, 0, 3], [0, 0, 0]].

Step 2: (ii) R2 - 2R1 = [0, -1, 5]; R3 - 3R1 = [0, -7, 4]; R3 - 7R2 = [0, 0, -31]. Echelon form: [[2, 3, -1], [0, -1, 5], [0, 0, -31]].

Step 3: (iii) R2 - 4R1 = [0, 17, -5]; R3 - 2R1 = [0, 7, 1]; R3 - (7/17)R2 = [0, 0, 52/17]. Echelon form: [[1, -3, 2], [0, 17, -5], [0, 0, 52/17]].

Step 4: (iv) R3 - 2R1 = [0, -2, -5]; R3 + (2/3)R2 = [0, 0, -11/3]. Echelon form: [[1, -1, 3], [0, 3, 2], [0, 0, -11/3]].

Answer: (i) [[1, 2, -1], [0, 0, 3], [0, 0, 0]]; (ii) [[2, 3, -1], [0, -1, 5], [0, 0, -31]]; (iii) [[1, -3, 2], [0, 17, -5], [0, 0, 52/17]]; (iv) [[1, -1, 3], [0, 3, 2], [0, 0, -11/3]]

Worked Example: 2. Reduce the following matrices into reduced echelon form. (i) [[1, 3, -2], [1, -4, 3], [3, 2, 1]]; (ii) [[1, -2, -3], [3, -1, 4], [4, 7, 3]]; (iii) [[3, 5, 4], [4, 1, 5], [7, 6, 3]]; (iv) [[0, 3, 2], [2, -4, 6], [2, 3, -1]].

Formula used: Row operations: swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero number, add a multiple of one row to another; A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|.

Step 1: (i) R2 - R1 = [0, -7, 5]; R3 - 3R1 = [0, -7, 7]; R3 - R2 = [0, 0, 2]. Pivots in all three columns; scaling and back-substitution give I_3.

Step 2: (ii) R2 - 3R1 = [0, 5, 13]; R3 - 4R1 = [0, 15, 15]; R3 - 3R2 = [0, 0, -24]. Three pivots; reduced form is I_3.

Step 3: (iii) R2 - (4/3)R1 and R3 - (7/3)R1, then elimination, give three pivots; reduced form is I_3.

Step 4: (iv) Swap R1 and R2, then eliminate below and above; three pivots; reduced form is I_3.

Answer: All four reduce to I_3

Worked Example: 3. Find rank by using row operations. (i) [[1, 2, 3], [2, 5, 4], [3, 0, 5]]; (ii) [[4, 2, 5], [-2, -3, 3], [-1, 3, 2]]; (iii) [[2, 1, 3], [0, 2, 1], [5, -3, 2]]; (iv) [[3, 6, 15], [0, 6, 2], [1, 2, 5]].

Formula used: Row operations: swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero number, add a multiple of one row to another; A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|.

Step 1: (i) Echelon form [[1, 2, 3], [0, 1, -2], [0, 0, -16]] has 3 non-zero rows: rank 3.

Step 2: (ii) Echelon form [[4, 2, 5], [0, -2, 11/2], [0, 0, 103/8]] has 3 non-zero rows: rank 3.

Step 3: (iii) Echelon form [[2, 1, 3], [0, 2, 1], [0, 0, -11/4]] has 3 non-zero rows: rank 3.

Step 4: (iv) Echelon form [[3, 6, 15], [0, 6, 2], [0, 0, 0]] has 2 non-zero rows: rank 2.

Answer: (i) 3; (ii) 3; (iii) 3; (iv) 2

Worked Example: 4. Find the inverse by using row operations and by adjoint method. (i) [[1, 2, -3], [0, 3, 0], [3, -2, 2]]; (ii) [[3, 5, 7], [4, 2, 1], [2, 0, 3]]; (iii) [[5, -2, -1], [0, 3, 2], [2, 1, 1]]; (iv) [[0, 1, 5], [2, 4, 3], [-3, -1, 6]].

Formula used: Row operations: swap rows, multiply a row by a non-zero number, add a multiple of one row to another; A^(-1) = adj(A) / |A|.

Step 1: (i) Determinant 33. Adjoint method: cofactors give adj = [[6, 2, 9], [0, 11, 0], [-9, 8, 3]]; dividing by 33 gives [[2/11, 2/33, 3/11], [0, 1/3, 0], [-3/11, 8/33, 1/11]]. Row reduction of [A | I] gives the same matrix.

Step 2: (ii) Determinant -60. Adjoint divided by -60 gives [[-1/10, 1/4, 3/20], [1/6, 1/12, -5/12], [1/15, -1/6, 7/30]]; row reduction of [A | I] agrees.

Step 3: (iii) Determinant 3. Adjoint divided by 3 gives [[1/3, 1/3, -1/3], [4/3, 7/3, -10/3], [-2, -3, 5]]; row reduction of [A | I] agrees.

Step 4: (iv) Determinant 29. Adjoint divided by 29 gives [[27/29, -11/29, -17/29], [-21/29, 15/29, 10/29], [10/29, -3/29, -2/29]]; row reduction of [A | I] agrees.

Answer: (i) [[2/11, 2/33, 3/11], [0, 1/3, 0], [-3/11, 8/33, 1/11]]; (ii) [[-1/10, 1/4, 3/20], [1/6, 1/12, -5/12], [1/15, -1/6, 7/30]]; (iii) [[1/3, 1/3, -1/3], [4/3, 7/3, -10/3], [-2, -3, 5]]; (iv) [[27/29, -11/29, -17/29], [-21/29, 15/29, 10/29], [10/29, -3/29, -2/29]]

lessons.title: Exercise 2.4 (p.84) - Solving Systems of Linear Equations
lessons.notes_html:
One system, many methods: homogeneous systems, consistency of non-homogeneous systems, the matrix inversion method, Cramer’s rule, Gaussian elimination (echelon form) and the Gauss-Jordan method (reduced echelon form). Check every solution by putting it back into the printed equations — some of the book’s printed answers are wrong, and the solved notes say so where it happens.

In this exercise: 1. Solve a system of homogeneous linear equations. 2. Solve the system of linear equation and also state that they are consistent or inconsistent system. 3. Solve the non-homogeneous linear equations using matrix inversion method. 4. Solve by Cramer's rule if possible. 5. Solve by Gaussian elimination method (echelon form). 6. Solve by Gauss Jordon method (reduced echelon form).

Worked Example: 1. Solve a system of homogeneous linear equations. (i) 2x + 4y + 6z = 0; 4x + 5y + 6z = 0; 3x + y - 2z = 0. (ii) 3x_1 - 4x_2 + 2x_3 = 0; -9x_1 + 12x_2 - 6x_3 = 0; -6x_1 + 8x_2 - 4x_3 = 0. (Flag for (ii): the book's Answers section says 'No Solution', which is impossible for a homogeneous system — it always has the trivial solution — and here all three equations are multiples of one another, so there are infinitely many solutions.)

Formula used: X = A^(-1) B; Cramer: x = Dx / D etc.; elimination: reduce [A | B] until the unknowns can be read off, from the last row upwards (Gaussian) or directly (Gauss-Jordan).

Step 1: (i) The coefficient matrix has rank 3 (determinant non-zero), so only the trivial solution x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 exists.

Step 2: (ii) Row 2 = -3 x row 1 and row 3 = -2 x row 1, so the system is just 3x_1 - 4x_2 + 2x_3 = 0: infinitely many solutions, e.g. x_1 = (4x_2 - 2x_3)/3 with x_2, x_3 free (including the trivial solution).

Answer: (i) x = 0, y = 0, z = 0 only; (ii) infinitely many solutions: 3x_1 - 4x_2 + 2x_3 = 0 (flag: book's Answers 'No Solution' is wrong — see steps)

Worked Example: 3. Solve the non-homogeneous linear equations using matrix inversion method. (i) 2x + y - z = 8; -3x - y + 2z = -11; -2x + y + 2z = -3. (ii) x_1 + 3x_2 + x_3 = 9; x_1 + x_2 - x_3 = 1; 3x_1 + 11x_2 + 5x_3 = 35. (iii) x + y - z = 1; -x + y - z = -1; x + y + z = 0. (Flags: for (ii) the book's Answers 'No solution' is wrong — equation 3 is satisfied identically by the family given (check: 3(-3 + 2t) + 11(4 - t) + 5t = 35). For (iii) the book's Answers (1/2, 1, -1/2) fails equation 1 (1/2 + 1 + 1/2 = 2, not 1) and equation 3 (1/2 + 1 - 1/2 = 1, not 0); the correct solution is (1, -1/2, -1/2).)

Formula used: X = A^(-1) B; Cramer: x = Dx / D etc.; elimination: reduce [A | B] until the unknowns can be read off, from the last row upwards (Gaussian) or directly (Gauss-Jordan).

Step 1: (i) The inverse of the coefficient matrix times (8, -11, -3) gives (2, 3, -1). Check: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8; -6 - 3 - 2 = -11; -4 + 3 - 2 = -3.

Step 2: (ii) Subtracting equations 1 and 2 gives x_2 + x_3 = 4; then x_1 = -3 + 2x_3 and x_2 = 4 - x_3, with x_3 free; equation 3 is then satisfied identically. Infinitely many solutions.

Step 3: (iii) Adding equations 1 and 2 gives y = z; equation 1 then gives x = 1; equation 3 gives 1 + 2y = 0, so y = z = -1/2. Solution (1, -1/2, -1/2).

Answer: (i) x = 2, y = 3, z = -1; (ii) infinitely many: x_1 = -3 + 2x_3, x_2 = 4 - x_3 (flag: book's Answers 'No solution' is wrong — see steps); (iii) x = 1, y = -1/2, z = -1/2 (flag: book's Answers (1/2, 1, -1/2) fails the equations — see steps)

Worked Example: 4. Solve by Cramer's rule if possible. (i) 2x + 3y + 3z = 5; x - 2y + z = -4; 3x - y - 2z = 3. (ii) x - y + z = 4; 2x + y - 3z = 0; x + y + z = 2. (iii) 9x_1 + 3x_2 + 4x_3 = 7; 4x_1 + 3x_2 + 4x_3 = 8; x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 3.

Formula used: X = A^(-1) B; Cramer: x = Dx / D etc.; elimination: reduce [A | B] until the unknowns can be read off, from the last row upwards (Gaussian) or directly (Gauss-Jordan).

Step 1: (i) D = 40; D_x = 40, D_y = 80, D_z = -40, so x = 1, y = 2, z = -1.

Step 2: (ii) D = 10; D_x = 20, D_y = -10, D_z = 10, so x = 2, y = -1, z = 1.

Step 3: (iii) D = -5; D_x = 1, D_y = -20, D_z = 4, so x_1 = -1/5, x_2 = 4, x_3 = -4/5.

Answer: (i) x = 1, y = 2, z = -1 (D = 40); (ii) x = 2, y = -1, z = 1 (D = 10); (iii) x_1 = -1/5, x_2 = 4, x_3 = -4/5 (D = -5)

Worked Example: 6. Solve by Gauss Jordon method (reduced echelon form). (i) x - 2y + z = -1; 3x + y - 2z = 4; y - z = 1. (ii) 2x_1 + x_2 + 3x_3 = 3; x_1 + x_2 - 2x_3 = 0; -3x_1 - x_2 + 2x_3 = -4. (iii) x + y = 2; 2x - z = 1; 2y - 3z = -1.

Formula used: X = A^(-1) B; Cramer: x = Dx / D etc.; elimination: reduce [A | B] until the unknowns can be read off, from the last row upwards (Gaussian) or directly (Gauss-Jordan).

Step 1: (i) Reduced echelon form is I with right side (1, 1, 0): x = 1, y = 1, z = 0.

Step 2: (ii) Reduced echelon form is I with right side (2, -8/5, 1/5): x_1 = 2, x_2 = -8/5, x_3 = 1/5.

Step 3: (iii) Reduced echelon form is I with right side (1, 1, 1): x = 1, y = 1, z = 1.

Answer: (i) x = 1, y = 1, z = 0; (ii) x_1 = 2, x_2 = -8/5, x_3 = 1/5; (iii) x = 1, y = 1, z = 1

lessons.title: Exercise 2.5 (pp.89-90) - Matrices at Work — Codes, Images and Transformations
lessons.notes_html:
Matrices in use: coding and decoding messages with an inverse matrix, images of triangles and squares under translations and transformations, a pixel image scaled by 0.5I, and a stiffness-matrix system K x = F solved for the displacements.

In this exercise: 1. Decode this cipher text that has been encoded using the matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: DPOOOHZZVOQOVYYVQQ. 2. Using matrix B = [[1, 1, -1], [1, 0, 1], [2, 1, 1]], encode the message: ATTACH NOW. 3. Decode the following message that was encoded using matrix B = [[1, 1, -1], [1, 0, 1], [2, 1, 1]]: [11; 20; 43], [25; 10; 41], [22; 14; 41]. 4. Find the image of triangle PQR with vertices P(2, -3), Q(0, 1) and R(-1, -2) under the translation vector [5; -1]. Sketch the original and image figures. 5. Find the images of the vertices of a unit square ABCD under the transformation given by L = [[1, 2], [-1, 1]]. The square has D(0, 0), C(1, 0), B(1, 1), A(0, 1). 6. An image is represented by a 2x2 matrix of pixel brightness values: I = [[120, 180], [200, 240]]. Find the new image matrix (Hint: find 0.5I). 7. A two-floor building has a stiffness matrix: K = [[10, -2], [-2, 5]] and F = [18; 11]. Find displacement solving the system of equations. (Hint: Find KF). 8. Point B = (1, 3) is scaled by 3 in x-direction and 2 in y-direction. Find new coordinate using S = [[3, 0], [0, 2]]. (Hint: Find SB).

Worked Example: 1. Decode this cipher text that has been encoded using the matrix A = [[2, 1], [1, 2]]: DPOOOHZZVOQOVYYVQQ. (Flag: the book never states the reduction step, but it is forced by the data — plain integer decoding gives fractions, while decoding modulo 26 (with 0 read as Z) gives a meaningful message, and re-encoding that message with A modulo 26 reproduces the cipher letter for letter. The final W is a padding letter, since the message has 17 letters and the code works in pairs.)

Formula used: Decode with A^(-1) and encode with A, working modulo 26 for letters; image of a point = transformation matrix x position vector (plus the translation vector for a translation).

Step 1: Convert letters to numbers (A = 1, ..., Z = 26) and pair them: (4, 16), (15, 15), (15, 8), (26, 26), (22, 15), (17, 15), (22, 25), (25, 22), (17, 17).

Step 2: The inverse of A modulo 26 is [[18, 17], [17, 18]] (since det(A) = 3 and 3 x 9 = 27 = 1 mod 26). Multiply each pair by it, modulo 26: (6, 18), (5, 5), (16, 9), (26, 26), (1, 20), (15, 13), (15, 18), (18, 15), (23, 23).

Step 3: Convert back to letters: F, R, E, E, P, I, Z, Z, A, T, O, M, O, R, R, O, W, W — i.e. 'FREE PIZZA TOMORROW' with a final padding W.

Answer: FREE PIZZA TOMORROW (see flag for the method and the padding letter)

Worked Example: 3. Decode the following message that was encoded using matrix B = [[1, 1, -1], [1, 0, 1], [2, 1, 1]]: [11; 20; 43], [25; 10; 41], [22; 14; 41].

Formula used: Decode with A^(-1) and encode with A, working modulo 26 for letters; image of a point = transformation matrix x position vector (plus the translation vector for a translation).

Step 1: The inverse of B is [[1, 2, -1], [-1, -3, 2], [-1, -1, 1]] (det(B) = -1).

Step 2: B^(-1) x (11, 20, 43) = (11 + 40 - 43, -11 - 60 + 86, -11 - 20 + 43) = (8, 15, 12) = H, O, L.

Step 3: B^(-1) x (25, 10, 41) = (25 + 20 - 41, -25 - 30 + 82, -25 - 10 + 41) = (4, 27, 6) = D, space, F (27 = space, as in Example 2.25).

Step 4: B^(-1) x (22, 14, 41) = (22 + 28 - 41, -22 - 42 + 82, -22 - 14 + 41) = (9, 18, 5) = I, R, E. Message: 'HOLD FIRE'.

Answer: HOLD FIRE

Worked Example: 5. Find the images of the vertices of a unit square ABCD under the transformation given by L = [[1, 2], [-1, 1]]. The square has D(0, 0), C(1, 0), B(1, 1), A(0, 1).

Formula used: Decode with A^(-1) and encode with A, working modulo 26 for letters; image of a point = transformation matrix x position vector (plus the translation vector for a translation).

Step 1: L x D = (0, 0), so D' = (0, 0). L x C = (1, -1), so C' = (1, -1). L x B = (1 + 2, -1 + 1) = (3, 0), so B' = (3, 0). L x A = (2, 1), so A' = (2, 1). The image is the parallelogram (0, 0), (1, -1), (3, 0), (2, 1).

Answer: A'(2, 1), B'(3, 0), C'(1, -1), D'(0, 0)

Worked Example: 6. An image is represented by a 2x2 matrix of pixel brightness values: I = [[120, 180], [200, 240]]. Find the new image matrix (Hint: find 0.5I).

Formula used: Decode with A^(-1) and encode with A, working modulo 26 for letters; image of a point = transformation matrix x position vector (plus the translation vector for a translation).

Step 1: 0.5I = [[60, 90], [100, 120]].

Answer: [[60, 90], [100, 120]]

Worked Example: 8. Point B = (1, 3) is scaled by 3 in x-direction and 2 in y-direction. Find new coordinate using S = [[3, 0], [0, 2]]. (Hint: Find SB).

Formula used: Decode with A^(-1) and encode with A, working modulo 26 for letters; image of a point = transformation matrix x position vector (plus the translation vector for a translation).

Step 1: S B = (3 x 1, 2 x 3) = (3, 6).

Answer: (3, 6)

lessons.title: Review Exercise 2 (pp.90-93)
lessons.notes_html:
Review of Unit 2: matrix types, determinants and adjoints, inverses, systems solved by inversion and Cramer’s rule, and images under translation.

In this exercise: 1. Choose the correct options. 2. Find the values of x and y from 2[[x, 5], [7, y - 3]] + [[3, -4], [1, 2]] = [[7, 6], [15, 14]]. 3. Calculate AC, BC and (A + B)C. Also verify that (A + B)C = AC + BC for A = [[0, 6, 7], [-6, 0, 8], [7, -8, 0]], B = [[0, 1, 1], [1, 0, 2], [1, 2, 0]], C = [2; -2; 3]. 4. If A = [[3, 1], [-1, 2]] show that A^2 - 5A + 7I = 0. 5. Show that |a, b, c; a + 2x, b + 2y, c + 2z; x, y, z| = 0. 6. Show that |x + y + 2z, x, y; z, y + z + 2x, y; z, x, z + x + 2y| = 2(x + y + z)^3. 7. Show that |sin(alpha), cos(alpha), cos(alpha + delta); sin(beta), cos(beta), cos(beta + delta); sin(gamma), cos(gamma), cos(gamma + delta)| = 0. 8. Solve the system of linear equations using matrix inversion method. 2x + 3y + 3z = 5; x - 2y + z = -4; 3x - y - 2z = 3. 9. Use Cramer's rule to solve the system: x + y + z = 4; 2x + y - z = 3; 3x + 3y + 2z = 10. 10. Find the image of triangle ABC with vertices A(3, 2), B(0, 5) and C(-3, -2) under the translation vector [2; -1], sketch the original and image figure.

Worked Example: 1(i). A matrix having 1-by-n order is called;

a) row matrix   b) column matrix   c) square matrix   d) diagonal matrix

Answer: a) row matrix

Worked Example: 1(ii). A square matrix with a_ij = 1 for i = j and a_ij = 0 for i not equal to j is called;

a) diagonal matrix   b) scalar matrix   c) unit matrix   d) none of these

Answer: c) unit matrix

Worked Example: 1(iii). Value of |1, 2, 3; 4, 5, 6; 1, 2, 3| is;

a) -1   b) 0   c) 1   d) 2

Answer: b) 0

Worked Example: 1(iv). Inverse of [[3, 4], [4, 5]] is;

a) [[3, 4], [-4, -5]]   b) [[-3, -4], [4, 5]]   c) [[5, 4], [4, 3]]   d) [[-5, 4], [4, -3]]

Answer: d) [[-5, 4], [4, -3]]

Worked Example: 1(v). Adjoint of [[2, 3], [-4, 5]] is

a) [[2, -3], [-4, 5]]   b) [[5, 3], [-4, 2]]   c) [[5, -3], [4, 2]]   d) [[5, -3], [4, -2]]

Answer: c) [[5, -3], [4, 2]]

Note: The book’s printed answer key says (d), but the adjoint is the transpose of the cofactor matrix [[5, 4], [-3, 2]], which is option (c) — the key is wrong.

Worked Example: 1(vi). In a row vector number of rows are

a) 1   b) 2   c) n   d) m

Answer: a) 1

Worked Example: 1(vii). Inverse of [[1, 2], [1, 3]] is

a) [[1, 1], [2, 3]]   b) [[1, 2], [3, 1]]   c) [[3, 2], [1, 1]]   d) [[3, -2], [-1, 1]]

Answer: d) [[3, -2], [-1, 1]]

Worked Example: 1(viii). Minor of an element of a square matrix is denoted by

a) M   b) M_ij   c) M_i   d) M_j

Answer: b) M_ij

Worked Example: 1(ix). Solution of system of linear equations is; x - 2y + z = 2; 2x + 2y - z = 4; x + y = 0. (From the third equation y = -x; the second gives z = -4; the first gives x = 2, y = -2.)

a) (2, 2, 4)   b) (2, -2, -4)   c) (-2, 2, -4)   d) (2, -2, 4)

Answer: b) (2, -2, -4)

Worked Example: 1(x). System of equations is called; a_1 x + b_1 y = K_1; a_2 x + b_2 y = K_2 where K_1 not equal to 0, K_2 not equal to 0

a) non-homogeneous   b) homogeneous   c) quadratic equations   d) cubic equations

Answer: a) non-homogeneous

Worked Example: 2. Find the values of x and y from 2[[x, 5], [7, y - 3]] + [[3, -4], [1, 2]] = [[7, 6], [15, 14]].

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 2 Overview and Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: Entry (1,1): 2x + 3 = 7, so x = 2. Entry (1,2): 10 - 4 = 6, which checks. Entry (2,1): 14 + 1 = 15, which checks. Entry (2,2): 2(y - 3) + 2 = 14, so y - 3 = 6 and y = 9.

Answer: x = 2, y = 9 (flag: book's answer key says y = 10, but 2(y - 3) + 2 = 14 gives y = 9)

Worked Example: 4. If A = [[3, 1], [-1, 2]] show that A^2 - 5A + 7I = 0.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 2 Overview and Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: A^2 = [[9 - 1, 3 + 2], [-3 - 2, -1 + 4]] = [[8, 5], [-5, 3]].

Step 2: 5A = [[15, 5], [-5, 10]] and 7I = [[7, 0], [0, 7]].

Step 3: A^2 - 5A + 7I = [[8 - 15 + 7, 5 - 5], [-5 + 5, 3 - 10 + 7]] = [[0, 0], [0, 0]].

Answer: A^2 - 5A + 7I = 0 is shown

Worked Example: 6. Show that |x + y + 2z, x, y; z, y + z + 2x, y; z, x, z + x + 2y| = 2(x + y + z)^3.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 2 Overview and Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: Every row sums to 2(x + y + z). Add columns 2 and 3 to column 1 and take 2(x + y + z) out; then row and column operations reduce the remaining determinant to (x + y + z)^2. Total: 2(x + y + z)^3.

Answer: 2(x + y + z)^3 is shown

Worked Example: 8. Solve the system of linear equations using matrix inversion method. 2x + 3y + 3z = 5; x - 2y + z = -4; 3x - y - 2z = 3.

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 2 Overview and Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: This is the same system as Exercise 2.4 Q4(i). Inverting the coefficient matrix and multiplying by (5, -4, 3) gives (1, 2, -1). Check: 2 + 6 - 3 = 5; 1 - 4 - 1 = -4; 3 - 2 + 2 = 3.

Answer: x = 1, y = 2, z = -1

Worked Example: 10. Find the image of triangle ABC with vertices A(3, 2), B(0, 5) and C(-3, -2) under the translation vector [2; -1], sketch the original and image figure. (Flag: a sketch question — the image triangle is given exactly. The book's answer key prints A'(15, 1); A(3, 2) + (2, -1) = (5, 1).)

Formula used: See the formulas in the Unit 2 Overview and Lessons 1 to 5 of this unit.

Step 1: Add (2, -1) to each vertex: A' = (3 + 2, 2 - 1) = (5, 1); B' = (0 + 2, 5 - 1) = (2, 4); C' = (-3 + 2, -2 - 1) = (-1, -3). Sketch both triangles from their vertices.

Answer: A'(5, 1), B'(2, 4), C'(-1, -3) (flag: book's answer key prints A'(15, 1) — a misprint for (5, 1))

lessons.title: Unit 3 Overview — Sequences and Series
lessons.notes_html:
A sequence lists numbers in order; a series adds them. In an arithmetic progression (A.P.) each term grows by a fixed common difference d; in a geometric progression (G.P.) each term is multiplied by a fixed common ratio r; in a harmonic progression (H.P.) the reciprocals of the terms form an A.P.

Between two numbers a and b sit three kinds of mean: the arithmetic mean A, the geometric mean G and the harmonic mean H, linked by G^2 = A x H.

Formula: A.P.: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d; S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (a1 + a_n)

Formula: G.P.: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1) for r not 1

Formula: Infinite G.P. (|r| < 1): S_inf = a1 / (1 - r)

Formula: Means between a and b: A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); H = 2ab / (a + b); and G^2 = A x H

Formula: H.P.: work with the reciprocals — they are in A.P.

Key Points

  • To insert n means between a and b, the A.P. (or G.P.) has n + 2 terms — find d (or r) from the last term first.
  • A recurring decimal is an infinite G.P.: split it into the non-recurring part plus a G.P. with ratio 1/10, 1/100, ...
  • Three numbers in A.P. are best taken as a - d, a, a + d; in G.P. as a/r, a, a r.
  • If S_n is given as a formula in n, the series itself comes from a_n = S_n - S_(n-1).
  • For an H.P. question, always change to the reciprocal A.P., solve there, and change back.

lessons.title: Exercise 3.1 (pp.97-98) - Arithmetic Sequences and the n-th Term
lessons.notes_html:
Finding indicated terms of an A.P. from a_n = a1 + (n - 1)d: read a1 and d from the sequence, or build two equations from two given terms and solve for them. The last questions prove identities about the u-th, v-th and w-th terms.

In this exercise: 1. Find the indicated terms of the following sequences. 2. Find the first four terms of the following arithmetic sequences, if. 3. If a_{n-3} = 9n - 4, find n-th term of the sequence. 4. Find 25th term of the sequence 1, 2 - y, 3 - 2y. 5. Find the 18th term of the A.P. if its 6th term is 11 and the 15th term is 47. 6. Which term of the sequence -15, -9, -3, ... is 75. 7. Which term of the sequence 5/7, 3/7, 1/7, ... is -105/7. 8. Find the n-th term of the sequence (6/7)^2, (11/7)^2, (16/7)^2. 9. If a, b, c are the u-th, v-th and w-th terms of an A.P., show that. 10. If 1/c, 1/d, 1/e are in A.P., show that the common difference is (c - e)/(2ce).

Worked Example: 1. Find the indicated terms of the following sequences. (i) 1, 5, 9, ..., a15; (ii) -15, -9, -3, ..., a10; (iii) -5, 4, 13, ..., a30; (iv) 23, 26, 29, ..., a14.

Formula used: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d; for two given terms, subtract their equations to remove a1 and find d.

Step 1: Use a_n = a_1 + (n - 1)d, where a_1 is the first term and d is the common difference.

Step 2: (i) a_1 = 1, d = 5 - 1 = 4. a_15 = 1 + (15 - 1)(4) = 1 + 56 = 57.

Step 3: (ii) a_1 = -15, d = -9 - (-15) = 6. a_10 = -15 + (10 - 1)(6) = -15 + 54 = 39.

Step 4: (iii) a_1 = -5, d = 4 - (-5) = 9. a_30 = -5 + (30 - 1)(9) = -5 + 261 = 256.

Step 5: (iv) a_1 = 23, d = 26 - 23 = 3. a_14 = 23 + (14 - 1)(3) = 23 + 39 = 62.

Answer: (i) 57; (ii) 39; (iii) 256; (iv) 62

Worked Example: 3. If a_{n-3} = 9n - 4, find n-th term of the sequence.

Formula used: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d; for two given terms, subtract their equations to remove a1 and find d.

Step 1: Let m = n - 3, so n = m + 3.

Step 2: Then a_m = 9(m + 3) - 4 = 9m + 27 - 4 = 9m + 23.

Step 3: Replacing m by n, the n-th term is a_n = 9n + 23.

Answer: a_n = 9n + 23

Worked Example: 5. Find the 18th term of the A.P. if its 6th term is 11 and the 15th term is 47.

Formula used: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d; for two given terms, subtract their equations to remove a1 and find d.

Step 1: Let the first term be a and the common difference be d.

Step 2: a_6 = a + 5d = 11 ... (1). a_15 = a + 14d = 47 ... (2).

Step 3: Subtract (1) from (2): 9d = 36, so d = 4.

Step 4: Put d = 4 in (1): a + 20 = 11, so a = -9.

Step 5: a_18 = a + 17d = -9 + 17(4) = -9 + 68 = 59.

Answer: 59

Worked Example: 8. Find the n-th term of the sequence (6/7)^2, (11/7)^2, (16/7)^2, ...

Formula used: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d; for two given terms, subtract their equations to remove a1 and find d.

Step 1: The bases form the sequence 6/7, 11/7, 16/7, ..., an A.P. with first term 6/7 and common difference 5/7.

Step 2: The n-th base = 6/7 + (n - 1)(5/7) = (6 + 5n - 5)/7 = (5n + 1)/7.

Step 3: Therefore the n-th term of the given sequence is the square of the n-th base.

Answer: a_n = ((5n + 1)/7)^2

Worked Example: 10. If 1/c, 1/d, 1/e are in A.P., show that the common difference is (c - e)/(2ce). (Note: the book writes the common difference with the same letter d as the middle denominator; here the common difference is called D to avoid confusion.)

Formula used: a_n = a1 + (n - 1) d; for two given terms, subtract their equations to remove a1 and find d.

Step 1: Since 1/c, 1/d, 1/e are in A.P., the difference of consecutive terms is constant: let it be D.

Step 2: Then 1/d - 1/c = D and 1/e - 1/d = D.

Step 3: Subtracting: (1/e - 1/d) - (1/d - 1/c) = 0 is not needed; instead add the two gaps: (1/e - 1/c) = 2D.

Step 4: But 1/e - 1/c = (c - e)/(ce). So 2D = (c - e)/(ce), giving D = (c - e)/(2ce).

Answer: Common difference = (c - e)/(2ce)

lessons.title: Exercise 3.2 (p.100) - Arithmetic Means
lessons.notes_html:
The A.M. between two numbers is their average; inserting several A.Ms. means building the A.P. that runs from the first number to the last, with d = (b - a) / (n + 1) for n inserted means.

In this exercise: 1. Find A.M. between. 2. If 3 and 8 are two A.Ms. between a and b, find a and b. 3. Insert three A.Ms. between 4 and 17. 4. Insert four A.Ms. between √(3) and 12/√(3). 5. Find six A.Ms. between -15 and 15. 6. Find n so that (x^{n+4} + y^{n+4})/(x^{n+3} + y^{n+3}) may be the A.M. between x and y. 7. Find the values of x if |1 0; 0 4| is the A.M. between |x 1; 1 x+2| and |1 0; 0 4|. (Determinants written row-wise.).

Worked Example: 1. Find A.M. between. (i) 9 and 16; (ii) 6 + 2 √(7) and 4 - 2 √(7); (iii) 3x + 2y and 5x - 6y; (iv) 3 + 4 √(3) i and 9 - 4 √(3) i; (v) 3x^2 - 5x + 6 and -x^2 + 7x - 4; (vi) 3x - 5 and 5x + 3.

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: The arithmetic mean (A.M.) between a and b is (a + b)/2.

Step 2: (i) (9 + 16)/2 = 25/2.

Step 3: (ii) (6 + 2 √(7) + 4 - 2 √(7))/2 = 10/2 = 5.

Step 4: (iii) (3x + 2y + 5x - 6y)/2 = (8x - 4y)/2 = 4x - 2y.

Step 5: (iv) (3 + 4 √(3) i + 9 - 4 √(3) i)/2 = 12/2 = 6.

Step 6: (v) (3x^2 - 5x + 6 - x^2 + 7x - 4)/2 = (2x^2 + 2x + 2)/2 = x^2 + x + 1.

Step 7: (vi) (3x - 5 + 5x + 3)/2 = (8x - 2)/2 = 4x - 1.

Answer: (i) 25/2; (ii) 5; (iii) 4x - 2y; (iv) 6; (v) x^2 + x + 1; (vi) 4x - 1

Worked Example: 3. Insert three A.Ms. between 4 and 17.

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Inserting three means gives 5 terms in A.P.: first term 4, fifth term 17.

Step 2: Let the common difference be d: 4 + 4d = 17, so 4d = 13, d = 13/4.

Step 3: The three means are: 4 + 13/4 = 29/4; 4 + 2(13/4) = 4 + 13/2 = 21/2; 4 + 3(13/4) = 55/4.

Answer: 29/4, 21/2, 55/4

Worked Example: 4. Insert four A.Ms. between √(3) and 12/√(3).

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Note 12/√(3) = 4 √(3). Inserting four means gives 6 terms in A.P.: first term √(3), sixth term 4 √(3).

Step 2: Let the common difference be d: √(3) + 5d = 4 √(3), so 5d = 3 √(3), d = (3 √(3))/5.

Step 3: The four means are: √(3) + (3 √(3))/5 = (8 √(3))/5; (11 √(3))/5; (14 √(3))/5; (17 √(3))/5.

Answer: (8 √(3))/5, (11 √(3))/5, (14 √(3))/5, (17 √(3))/5

Worked Example: 5. Find six A.Ms. between -15 and 15.

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Inserting six means gives 8 terms in A.P.: first term -15, eighth term 15.

Step 2: Let the common difference be d: -15 + 7d = 15, so 7d = 30, d = 30/7.

Step 3: The six means are: -15 + 30/7 = -75/7; -45/7; -15/7; 15/7; 45/7; 75/7.

Answer: -75/7, -45/7, -15/7, 15/7, 45/7, 75/7

Worked Example: 7. Find the values of x if |1 0; 0 4| is the A.M. between |x 1; 1 x+2| and |1 0; 0 4|. (Determinants written row-wise.)

Formula used: A.M. = (a + b) / 2; n means between a and b: d = (b - a) / (n + 1).

Step 1: Evaluate the determinants: |1 0; 0 4| = 4; |x 1; 1 x+2| = x(x + 2) - 1 = x^2 + 2x - 1; the third determinant is again 4.

Step 2: The A.M. condition gives: 4 = ((x^2 + 2x - 1) + 4)/2.

Step 3: So x^2 + 2x + 3 = 8, i.e. x^2 + 2x - 5 = 0.

Step 4: By the quadratic formula: x = (-2 +- √(4 + 20))/2 = -1 +- √(6).

Answer: x = -1 + √(6) or x = -1 - √(6)

lessons.title: Exercise 3.3 (pp.103-104) - Sum of an Arithmetic Series
lessons.notes_html:
Summing an A.P. with S_n = (n/2)[2a1 + (n - 1)d]. Watch the questions that ask for the number of terms — they give a quadratic in n, and only the sensible positive root counts.

In this exercise: 1. Sum the series. 2. Find the number of terms of the following. 3. Sum the series. 4. If S_n = n(2n + 1), then find the series. 5. Find the sum of first 600 natural numbers which are neither divisible by 2 nor by 5. 6. If S_{3n}, S_{5n}, S_{8n} are the sums of 3n, 5n and 8n terms of a_n in A.P., show that S_{8n} = 4(S_{5n} - S_{3n}). 7. The sums of n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio of 4n - 3 : 2n + 1. Find the ratio of their 7th terms.

Worked Example: 1. Sum the series. (i) 3 + 7 + 11 + ... + a15; (ii) 4.57 + 4.87 + 5.17 + ... + a24; (iii) 3/√(2) + 2 √(2) + 5/√(2) + ... to n terms; (iv) (y - 3b) + (y - b) + (y + b) + ... to n terms; (v) 1/(1 - √(x)) + 1/(1 - x) + 1/(1 + √(x)) + ... to n terms; (vi) 2/√(3) + √(3) + 4/√(3) + ... + a20.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: Use S_n = (n/2)[2a + (n - 1)d].

Step 2: (i) a = 3, d = 4, n = 15: S_15 = (15/2)[6 + 14(4)] = (15/2)(62) = 465.

Step 3: (ii) a = 4.57, d = 0.30, n = 24: S_24 = 12[9.14 + 23(0.30)] = 12(16.04) = 192.48.

Step 4: (iii) a = 3/√(2), d = 2 √(2) - 3/√(2) = 1/√(2). S_n = (n/2)[6/√(2) + (n - 1)/√(2)] = n(n + 5)/(2 √(2)) = n(n + 5) √(2)/4.

Step 5: (iv) a = y - 3b, d = 2b. S_n = (n/2)[2(y - 3b) + (n - 1)(2b)] = (n/2)[2y + 2b(n - 4)] = ny + nb(n - 4).

Step 6: (v) Let t = √(x). The terms are 1/(1 - t), 1/(1 - t^2), 1/(1 + t); consecutive differences are both -t/(1 - t^2), so d = -√(x)/(1 - x) and a = 1/(1 - √(x)). S_n = (n/2)[2/(1 - t) + (n - 1)(-t/(1 - t^2))] = n[2 + (3 - n) √(x)]/[2(1 - x)].

Step 7: (vi) a = 2/√(3), d = √(3) - 2/√(3) = 1/√(3). a_20 = 2/√(3) + 19/√(3) = 21/√(3) = 7 √(3). S_20 = 10(2/√(3) + 7 √(3)) = 10(23/√(3)) = 230/√(3) = 230 √(3)/3.

Answer: (i) 465; (ii) 192.48; (iii) n(n + 5) √(2)/4; (iv) ny + nb(n - 4); (v) n[2 + (3 - n) √(x)]/[2(1 - x)]; (vi) 230 √(3)/3

Worked Example: 3. Sum the series. (i) 3 + 5 - 7 + 10 + 12 - 14 + 17 + 19 - 21 + ... to 3n terms. (ii) 9 + 12 - 15 + 18 + 21 - 24 + 27 + 30 - 33 + ... to 3n terms.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: (i) Group in threes: (3, 5, -7), (10, 12, -14), ... The k-th group is (7k - 4) + (7k - 2) + (-7k) = 7k - 6. Check: k = 1 gives 1 = 3 + 5 - 7; k = 2 gives 8 = 10 + 12 - 14.

Step 2: Sum over k = 1 to n: 7[n(n + 1)/2] - 6n = (7n^2 - 5n)/2 = n(7n - 5)/2.

Step 3: (ii) Group in threes: (9, 12, -15), (18, 21, -24), ... The k-th group is 9k + (9k + 3) - (9k + 6) = 9k - 3. Check: k = 1 gives 6 = 9 + 12 - 15; k = 2 gives 15 = 18 + 21 - 24.

Step 4: Sum over k = 1 to n: 9[n(n + 1)/2] - 3n = (9n^2 + 3n)/2 = 3n(3n + 1)/2.

Answer: (i) n(7n - 5)/2; (ii) 3n(3n + 1)/2

Worked Example: 4. If S_n = n(2n + 1), then find the series.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: The n-th term is a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} for n >= 2, and a_1 = S_1.

Step 2: S_1 = 1(3) = 3, so a_1 = 3.

Step 3: S_n - S_{n-1} = (2n^2 + n) - [2(n - 1)^2 + (n - 1)] = (2n^2 + n) - (2n^2 - 3n + 1) = 4n - 1.

Step 4: Hence a_n = 4n - 1: the series is 3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + ... Check: S_3 = 3(7) = 21 = 3 + 7 + 11.

Answer: The series is 3 + 7 + 11 + 15 + ... (a_n = 4n - 1)

Worked Example: 5. Find the sum of first 600 natural numbers which are neither divisible by 2 nor by 5.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: Among 1 to 600, the numbers neither divisible by 2 nor by 5 are the odd numbers not divisible by 5.

Step 2: Odd numbers from 1 to 600: 300 numbers, their sum = 300^2 = 90000 (sum of the first 300 odd numbers).

Step 3: Odd multiples of 5 among them: 5, 15, ..., 595, which are 60 numbers; their sum = 5(1 + 3 + ... + 119) = 5(60^2) = 18000.

Step 4: Required sum = 90000 - 18000 = 72000. Cross-check by inclusion-exclusion: 180300 - 90300 - 36300 + 18300 = 72000.

Answer: 72000

Worked Example: 7. The sums of n terms of two arithmetic series are in the ratio of 4n - 3 : 2n + 1. Find the ratio of their 7th terms.

Formula used: S_n = (n/2) [2a1 + (n - 1) d] = (n/2) (first term + last term).

Step 1: For an A.P., the sum of the first (2m - 1) terms equals (2m - 1) times the m-th term, so the ratio of the m-th terms equals the ratio of the sums of (2m - 1) terms.

Step 2: For m = 7: 2m - 1 = 13. Ratio of 7th terms = [4(13) - 3] : [2(13) + 1] = 49 : 27.

Answer: 49 : 27

lessons.title: Exercise 3.4 (p.106) - Geometric Sequences and the n-th Term
lessons.notes_html:
Finding terms of a G.P. from a_n = a1 r^(n - 1): divide two known terms to get a power of r. One question proves that the reciprocals of a G.P.’s terms again form a G.P.

In this exercise: 1. Find the indicated terms of the following G.P. 2. In a G.P., a_1 = 5/9, a_6 = 15625/9. Find its n-th term. 3. Find the n-th term of the geometric sequence if a_7/a_9 = 16/9 and a_2 = 9/4. 4. Show that the reciprocals of the terms of the G.P. 1/a_1, 1/(a_1 r^2), 1/(a_1 r^4), ... form another G.P. Also find the common ratio of the new G.P. 5. How many terms are in G.P. 1/3, 1/12, 1/48, ..., 1/196608. 6. If 1/(xy), 1/(yz), 1/(zx) are in G.P., show that x = +- √(yz).

Worked Example: 1. Find the indicated terms of the following G.P. (i) 2, 6, 18, ..., a7; (ii) 1 + i, 2(1 - i), ..., a10; (iii) 4, 2 √(2), 2, ..., a15; (iv) a^2 - b^2, a + b, (a + b)/(a - b), ..., a9.

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: Use a_n = a_1 r^{n-1}.

Step 2: (i) a_1 = 2, r = 3. a_7 = 2(3^6) = 2(729) = 1458.

Step 3: (ii) a_1 = 1 + i, r = 2(1 - i)/(1 + i) = (1 - i)^2 = -2i. (-2i)^9 = (-2)^9 i^9 = -512i. So a_10 = (1 + i)(-512i) = -512i + 512 = 512 - 512i.

Step 4: (iii) a_1 = 4, r = (2 √(2))/4 = 1/√(2). a_15 = 4(1/√(2))^{14} = 4/2^7 = 4/128 = 1/32.

Step 5: (iv) a_1 = a^2 - b^2, r = (a + b)/(a^2 - b^2) = 1/(a - b). a_9 = (a^2 - b^2)(1/(a - b))^8 = (a - b)(a + b)/(a - b)^8 = (a + b)/(a - b)^7.

Answer: (i) 1458; (ii) 512 - 512i; (iii) 1/32; (iv) (a + b)/(a - b)^7

Worked Example: 3. Find the n-th term of the geometric sequence if a_7/a_9 = 16/9 and a_2 = 9/4.

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: a_7/a_9 = 1/r^2 = 16/9, so r^2 = 9/16 and r = 3/4 or r = -3/4.

Step 2: a_2 = a_1 r = 9/4. If r = 3/4, then a_1 = 3 and a_n = 3(3/4)^{n-1}. If r = -3/4, then a_1 = -3 and a_n = -3(-3/4)^{n-1}. Both satisfy the given data.

Answer: a_n = 3(3/4)^{n-1} or a_n = -3(-3/4)^{n-1}

Worked Example: 4. Show that the reciprocals of the terms of the G.P. 1/a_1, 1/(a_1 r^2), 1/(a_1 r^4), ... form another G.P. Also find the common ratio of the new G.P.

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: The reciprocals of the terms are: 1/(1/a_1) = a_1; 1/(1/(a_1 r^2)) = a_1 r^2; 1/(1/(a_1 r^4)) = a_1 r^4; and so on.

Step 2: Each term divided by the previous one gives (a_1 r^2)/a_1 = r^2 and (a_1 r^4)/(a_1 r^2) = r^2, a constant.

Step 3: Hence the reciprocals form a G.P. with first term a_1 and common ratio r^2.

Answer: The reciprocals form a G.P. with common ratio r^2

Worked Example: 6. If 1/(xy), 1/(yz), 1/(zx) are in G.P., show that x = +- √(yz).

Formula used: a_n = a1 r^(n - 1); a_m / a_n = r^(m - n).

Step 1: In a G.P., the square of the middle term equals the product of the neighbouring terms: (1/(yz))^2 = (1/(xy))(1/(zx)).

Step 2: So 1/(y^2 z^2) = 1/(x^2 y z). Cross-multiplying: x^2 y z = y^2 z^2.

Step 3: Divide by yz (non-zero): x^2 = yz, so x = +- √(yz).

Answer: x = +- √(yz) is proved

lessons.title: Exercise 3.5 (p.109) - Geometric Means
lessons.notes_html:
The G.M. between two numbers is the square root of their product (same sign); inserting n G.Ms. builds a G.P. with r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)). One question links the A.M. and G.M. of two numbers back to the numbers themselves.

In this exercise: 1. Find G.M. between. 2. Insert two G.Ms. between 3 and 81. 3. Insert five G.Ms. between 16 and 1024. 4. Insert six G.Ms. between 9 and 19683. 5. The A.M. between two numbers is 17 and the geometric mean is 15, find the numbers. 6. For what value of n, is (x^{n-2} + y^{n-2})/(x^{n-3} + y^{n-3}) the G.M. between x and y. 7. Show that the n-th root of the product of n geometric means between a and b is the geometric mean between a and b.

Worked Example: 1. Find G.M. between: (i) 4 and 9; (ii) 4 √(5) and 5 √(5); (iii) 5 + i and 5 - i; (iv) 16/9 and 9/25.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: The geometric mean between a and b is G = +- √(ab).

Step 2: (i) +- √(4 x 9) = +- √(36) = +-6.

Step 3: (ii) +- √(4 √(5) x 5 √(5)) = +- √(100) = +-10.

Step 4: (iii) +- √((5 + i)(5 - i)) = +- √(26).

Step 5: (iv) +- √((16/9)(9/25)) = +- √(16/25) = +-4/5.

Answer: (i) +-6; (ii) +-10; (iii) +-√(26); (iv) +-4/5

Worked Example: 3. Insert five G.Ms. between 16 and 1024.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Inserting five means gives 7 terms in G.P.: first term 16, seventh term 1024.

Step 2: So 16r^6 = 1024, r^6 = 64, r = 2 or r = -2.

Step 3: With r = 2 the means are 32, 64, 128, 256, 512. With r = -2 they are -32, 64, -128, 256, -512. (The book's worked example uses the positive root.)

Answer: With r = 2: 32, 64, 128, 256, 512; with r = -2: -32, 64, -128, 256, -512

Worked Example: 4. Insert six G.Ms. between 9 and 19683.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Inserting six means gives 8 terms in G.P.: first term 9, eighth term 19683.

Step 2: So 9r^7 = 19683, r^7 = 2187 = 3^7, r = 3.

Step 3: The six means are 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187, 6561.

Answer: 27, 81, 243, 729, 2187, 6561

Worked Example: 5. The A.M. between two numbers is 17 and the geometric mean is 15, find the numbers.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Let the numbers be a and b. Then (a + b)/2 = 17, so a + b = 34; and √(ab) = 15, so ab = 225.

Step 2: Thus a and b are the roots of t^2 - 34t + 225 = 0.

Step 3: Discriminant = 34^2 - 4(225) = 1156 - 900 = 256 = 16^2. So t = (34 +- 16)/2 = 25 or 9.

Step 4: The numbers are 25 and 9.

Answer: 25 and 9

Worked Example: 7. Show that the n-th root of the product of n geometric means between a and b is the geometric mean between a and b.

Formula used: G.M. = √(a b) (for positive a, b); n means between a and b: r = (b / a)^(1 / (n + 1)).

Step 1: Let G_1, ..., G_n be the n geometric means between a and b. Then a, G_1, ..., G_n, b are in G.P. with n + 2 terms.

Step 2: Let r be the common ratio: b = a r^{n+1}, so r^{n+1} = b/a, and G_k = a r^k.

Step 3: The product G_1 ... G_n = (a r)(a r^2)...(a r^n) = a^n r^{1+2+...+n} = a^n r^{n(n+1)/2}.

Step 4: Its n-th root is a r^{(n+1)/2} = a (r^{n+1})^{1/2} = a (b/a)^{1/2} = √(ab), which is the geometric mean between a and b.

Answer: The n-th root of the product is √(ab), the G.M. between a and b

lessons.title: Exercise 3.6 (pp.114-115) - Sum of a Geometric Series and Recurring Decimals
lessons.notes_html:
Summing finite and infinite G.Ps. An infinite sum exists only when |r| < 1, and that is exactly what turns a recurring decimal into a vulgar fraction. The last questions reverse the process: from a given sum, find the series.

In this exercise: 1. Compute the sum. 2. Sum to n terms, the series. 3. If a_n = (1/4)^n then find its sum up to n terms. 4. Find the sums of the following infinite geometric series. 5. Find the vulgar fraction equivalent to the following recurring decimals (dots verified at 300 dpi: the repetend is the block under the dots). 6. If x = y/2 + y^2/4 + y^3/8 + ... if 0 < y < 2, prove that y = 2x/(1 + x). 7. If x = 3y/2 + 9y^2/4 + 27y^3/8 + ... if 0 < y < 2/3, then prove that y = 2x/[3(1 + x)]. 8. The sum of an infinite geometric series is one third the sum of the squares of its terms. If the sum of its first two terms is 3/4, find the series.

Worked Example: 1. Compute the sum. (i) 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + ... + 1/512; (ii) 2^6 + 2^7 + 2^8 + ... + 2^13; (iii) 1/u + 1/u^2 + 1/u^3 + ... + 1/u^8; (iv) 9 + 3 + 1 + ... + 1/2187; (v) 0.9 + 0.99 + 0.999 + ... to n terms; (vi) 7 + 77 + 777 + ... to n terms.

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: Use S_n = a(1 - r^n)/(1 - r) for r different from 1.

Step 2: (i) a = 1, r = 1/2, n = 10 (since 1/512 = (1/2)^9 is the 10th term). S = (1 - (1/2)^10)/(1/2) = 2(1 - 1/1024) = 1023/512.

Step 3: (ii) a = 64, r = 2, n = 8. S = 64(2^8 - 1)/(2 - 1) = 64(255) = 16320.

Step 4: (iii) a = 1/u, r = 1/u, n = 8. S = (1/u)(1 - u^{-8})/(1 - 1/u) = (u^8 - 1)/(u^8 (u - 1)).

Step 5: (iv) a = 9, r = 1/3. The last term 9(1/3)^{n-1} = 1/2187 = 3^{-7} gives n = 10. S = 9(1 - (1/3)^10)/(2/3) = (27/2)(59048/59049) = 29524/2187.

Step 6: (v) The k-th term is 1 - (1/10)^k. Sum = n - (1/10)(1 - (1/10)^n)/(9/10) = n - (1/9)(1 - 10^{-n}) = n - 1/9 + 10^{-n}/9.

Step 7: (vi) The k-th term is 7(10^k - 1)/9. Sum = (7/9)[10(10^n - 1)/9 - n] = 70(10^n - 1)/81 - 7n/9.

Answer: (i) 1023/512; (ii) 16320; (iii) (u^8 - 1)/(u^8 (u - 1)); (iv) 29524/2187; (v) n - 1/9 + 10^{-n}/9; (vi) 70(10^n - 1)/81 - 7n/9

Worked Example: 3. If a_n = (1/4)^n then find its sum up to n terms.

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: The series is 1/4 + (1/4)^2 + ... + (1/4)^n, a G.P. with a = 1/4, r = 1/4.

Step 2: Sum = (1/4)(1 - (1/4)^n)/(1 - 1/4) = (1/4)(1 - 4^{-n})/(3/4) = (1/3)(1 - 4^{-n}).

Answer: (1/3)(1 - 4^{-n})

Worked Example: 5. Find the vulgar fraction equivalent to the following recurring decimals (dots verified at 300 dpi: the repetend is the block under the dots). (i) 1.5454... (ii) 0.267267... (iii) 1.14848... (iv) 1.6666... (v) 3.26767... (vi) 1.45757...

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: Write each recurring decimal as a geometric series and sum it, or use the standard rule: repetend over as many 9s, with non-repeating part adjusted.

Step 2: (i) 1.5454... = 1 + 54/99 = 1 + 6/11 = 17/11.

Step 3: (ii) 0.267267... = 267/999 = 89/333.

Step 4: (iii) 1.14848... = 1.1 + 48/990 = 11/10 + 8/165 = 379/330.

Step 5: (iv) 1.6666... = 1 + 6/9 = 5/3.

Step 6: (v) 3.26767... = 3.2 + 67/990 = 16/5 + 67/990 = 647/198.

Step 7: (vi) 1.45757... = 1.4 + 57/990 = 7/5 + 57/990 = 481/330.

Answer: (i) 17/11; (ii) 89/333; (iii) 379/330; (iv) 5/3; (v) 647/198; (vi) 481/330

Worked Example: 6. If x = y/2 + y^2/4 + y^3/8 + ... if 0 < y < 2, prove that y = 2x/(1 + x).

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: The series is geometric with first term y/2 and ratio y/2. Since 0 < y < 2, |y/2| < 1, so it converges.

Step 2: Its sum is x = (y/2)/(1 - y/2) = y/(2 - y).

Step 3: Then x(2 - y) = y, i.e. 2x - xy = y, so 2x = y(1 + x), giving y = 2x/(1 + x).

Answer: y = 2x/(1 + x) is proved

Worked Example: 8. The sum of an infinite geometric series is one third the sum of the squares of its terms. If the sum of its first two terms is 3/4, find the series.

Formula used: S_n = a1 (r^n - 1) / (r - 1); S_inf = a1 / (1 - r) when |r| < 1; recurring block of length k gives ratio 1 / 10^k.

Step 1: Let the first term be a and the ratio be r, |r| < 1. Sum of the series = a/(1 - r).

Step 2: The squares form a G.P. with first term a^2 and ratio r^2; their sum = a^2/(1 - r^2).

Step 3: Given: a/(1 - r) = (1/3) a^2/(1 - r^2) = (1/3) a^2/[(1 - r)(1 + r)]. Cancelling a/(1 - r) (non-zero) gives 1 = a/[3(1 + r)], so a = 3(1 + r).

Step 4: Also a + ar = a(1 + r) = 3/4. Substituting a: 3(1 + r)^2 = 3/4, so (1 + r)^2 = 1/4, 1 + r = +-1/2.

Step 5: r = -3/2 is rejected (|r| >= 1, the infinite sum would not exist). Hence r = -1/2 and a = 3(1/2) = 3/2.

Step 6: The series is 3/2 - 3/4 + 3/8 - ... Check: sum = (3/2)/(3/2) = 1, and sum of squares = (9/4)/(3/4) = 3 = 3(1).

Answer: The series is 3/2 - 3/4 + 3/8 - ... (a = 3/2, r = -1/2)

lessons.title: Exercise 3.7 (p.117) - Harmonic Sequences and the n-th Term
lessons.notes_html:
An H.P. is handled through its reciprocal A.P.: invert every term, use a_n = a1 + (n - 1)d there, and invert the answer back.

In this exercise: 1. Find the n-th term of the H.P. 2. Find the 10th terms of the following harmonic sequences. 3. If the 7th and 10th terms of a H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21 respectively, find its 20th term. 4. If the numbers 1/u, 1/(2u + 1) and 1/(4u - 1) are in H.P., find u. 5. If the sum of first and sixth terms of H.P. is 31/116, find the sequence if the first term is 1/4. 6. In a harmonic progression, 5th and 9th terms are 7/30 and 7/54 respectively, find the 15th term.

Worked Example: 1. Find the n-th term of the H.P. (i) 1/3, 1/7, 1/11, ... (ii) 9/5, 9/13, 9/21, ...

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: For an H.P., the reciprocals of the terms form an A.P.; find the n-th term of that A.P. and take its reciprocal.

Step 2: (i) Reciprocals: 3, 7, 11, ... with a = 3, d = 4. The n-th reciprocal is 3 + (n - 1)(4) = 4n - 1. Hence the n-th term of the H.P. is 1/(4n - 1).

Step 3: (ii) Reciprocals: 5/9, 13/9, 21/9, ... with a = 5/9, d = 8/9. The n-th reciprocal is 5/9 + (n - 1)(8/9) = (8n - 3)/9. Hence the n-th term of the H.P. is 9/(8n - 3).

Answer: (i) 1/(4n - 1); (ii) 9/(8n - 3)

Worked Example: 3. If the 7th and 10th terms of a H.P. are 1/3 and 5/21 respectively, find its 20th term.

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: Work with reciprocals, which form an A.P. The 7th reciprocal is 3 and the 10th reciprocal is 21/5.

Step 2: Let the A.P. have first term a and difference d: a + 6d = 3 and a + 9d = 21/5.

Step 3: Subtracting: 3d = 21/5 - 3 = 6/5, so d = 2/5. Then a = 3 - 6(2/5) = 3/5.

Step 4: The 20th reciprocal is 3/5 + 19(2/5) = 41/5. Hence the 20th term of the H.P. is 5/41.

Answer: 5/41

Worked Example: 4. If the numbers 1/u, 1/(2u + 1) and 1/(4u - 1) are in H.P., find u.

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: The reciprocals u, 2u + 1, 4u - 1 must be in A.P.

Step 2: So twice the middle term equals the sum of the extremes: 2(2u + 1) = u + (4u - 1).

Step 3: Thus 4u + 2 = 5u - 1, giving u = 3.

Answer: u = 3

Worked Example: 6. In a harmonic progression, 5th and 9th terms are 7/30 and 7/54 respectively, find the 15th term.

Formula used: If 1/a_n is in A.P., then a_n is in H.P.; n-th term of the H.P. = 1 / (n-th term of the reciprocal A.P.).

Step 1: Work with reciprocals: the 5th reciprocal is 30/7 and the 9th reciprocal is 54/7.

Step 2: Let the A.P. have first term a and difference d: a + 4d = 30/7 and a + 8d = 54/7.

Step 3: Subtracting: 4d = 24/7, so d = 6/7. Then a = 30/7 - 4(6/7) = 6/7.

Step 4: The 15th reciprocal is 6/7 + 14(6/7) = 90/7. Hence the 15th term of the H.P. is 7/90.

Answer: 7/90

lessons.title: Exercise 3.8 (p.122) - Harmonic Means and the Three Means
lessons.notes_html:
The H.M. between a and b is 2ab / (a + b) — the reciprocal of the A.M. of the reciprocals. Inserting H.Ms. is done in the reciprocal A.P., and the final question checks G^2 = A x H.

In this exercise: 1. Find H.Ms. between the following numbers. 2. Insert four H.Ms. between 1/9 and 1/81. 3. Insert six H.Ms. between 1/12 and 1/48. 4. Find n so that (a^{n-5} + b^{n-5})/(a^{n-6} + b^{n-6}) may be H.M. between a and b. 5. Find A, G and H and show that G^2 = A x H, if.

Worked Example: 1. Find H.Ms. between the following numbers. (i) 4 and 9; (ii) 3 + √(2) and 3 - √(2); (iii) 2 + 3i and 2 - 3i; (iv) 1/7 and 1/11.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: The harmonic mean between a and b is H = 2ab/(a + b).

Step 2: (i) 2(4)(9)/(4 + 9) = 72/13.

Step 3: (ii) ab = (3 + √(2))(3 - √(2)) = 7, a + b = 6. H = 2(7)/6 = 7/3.

Step 4: (iii) ab = (2 + 3i)(2 - 3i) = 13, a + b = 4. H = 2(13)/4 = 13/2.

Step 5: (iv) ab = 1/77, a + b = 18/77. H = 2(1/77)/(18/77) = 2/18 = 1/9.

Answer: (i) 72/13; (ii) 7/3; (iii) 13/2; (iv) 1/9

Worked Example: 2. Insert four H.Ms. between 1/9 and 1/81.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: Work with reciprocals: they form an A.P. with 6 terms, first term 9, sixth term 81.

Step 2: Let the difference be d: 9 + 5d = 81, so d = 72/5.

Step 3: The reciprocals of the four means are 9 + 72/5 = 117/5, 189/5, 261/5, 333/5.

Step 4: Taking reciprocals, the four H.Ms. are 5/117, 5/189, 5/261, 5/333.

Answer: 5/117, 5/189, 5/261, 5/333

Worked Example: 4. Find n so that (a^{n-5} + b^{n-5})/(a^{n-6} + b^{n-6}) may be H.M. between a and b.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: The H.M. between a and b is 2ab/(a + b). Put m = n - 6, so the expression is (a^{m+1} + b^{m+1})/(a^m + b^m).

Step 2: Set it equal to 2ab/(a + b) and cross-multiply: (a + b)(a^{m+1} + b^{m+1}) = 2ab(a^m + b^m).

Step 3: Expand: a^{m+2} + a b^{m+1} + a^{m+1} b + b^{m+2} = 2a^{m+1} b + 2a b^{m+1}.

Step 4: Rearrange: a^{m+2} - a^{m+1} b - a b^{m+1} + b^{m+2} = (a - b)(a^{m+1} - b^{m+1}) = 0.

Step 5: For a different from b this holds identically only when m + 1 = 0, i.e. m = -1. Hence n = 5.

Step 6: Check: for n = 5 the expression is (1 + 1)/(1/a + 1/b) = 2ab/(a + b).

Answer: n = 5

Worked Example: 5. Find A, G and H and show that G^2 = A x H, if (i) a = 12, b = 3; (ii) a = 2/5, b = 8/5.

Formula used: H.M. = 2ab / (a + b); A = (a + b) / 2; G = √(a b); G^2 = A x H.

Step 1: Use A = (a + b)/2, G = √(ab), H = 2ab/(a + b).

Step 2: (i) A = (12 + 3)/2 = 15/2; G = √(36) = 6; H = 2(36)/15 = 24/5. Then A x H = (15/2)(24/5) = 36 = G^2.

Step 3: (ii) A = (2/5 + 8/5)/2 = 1; G = √(16/25) = 4/5; H = 2(16/25)/(10/5) = 16/25. Then A x H = 16/25 = G^2.
